activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The phone call came on a Tuesday evening while Maika was reheating rice at the kitchen counter. The manager of Halloran's Grocery said she could start Saturday, eight hours, minimum wage, and that she should pick up her paperwork before then. She said thank you twice, hung up, and stood for a moment with her hand still on the microwave door, as if the job might evaporate if she moved.

The paperwork turned out to be a stapled packet, and the last page was a sheet of federal child labor rules she had to sign. She read it at the kitchen table on Thursday night while her mother watched something with the volume too low in the next room. Most of it was predictable: no work during school hours, limits on hours during the school week. But one line stopped her. Workers under eighteen may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. She read it three times, then copied it into the back of her chemistry notebook, the way she did with things she wanted to internalize rather than just remember. Under eighteen. Not her specifically, not a suggestion. Anyone.

Romain had gotten her the referral in the first place. He was seventeen, had been at Halloran's since June, and had texted her that afternoon: orientation is a joke, the manager is saturnine but harmless, just nod a lot. He arrived at her door Friday after his shift, still smelling faintly of the hot case, and did not sit down when she offered the chair.

"Problem," he said. "Frank asked me to cover the deli tomorrow. The usual guy called in sick. Slicer, scale, the whole station."

"You can't," Maika said. She turned her notebook around on the table so he could see what she'd copied.

He read it, and his jaw worked the way it did before he argued with a teacher. "That's a rule for, like, factories."

"It says even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. It says under eighteen. It's a federal thing."

"Frank doesn't care about federal things. He cares that the case is full by ten a.m." Romain picked up a pen from the table and put it down again without using it. "Everyone covers the slicer. The last new kid did. It's a truism around there, you just do what's short-handed."

Delphine, consulted by group chat, was blunter. dont make it weird, she typed. its one shift. half the stuff on those sheets nobody follows. Maika stared at the message long enough that the screen dimmed. There was something in Delphine's position she couldn't dismiss: the rules existed on paper, and the store existed in the world, and the world ran on covering for people, on being useful, on not being the sixteen-year-old who quotes federal regulations at a man who controlled the schedule. Wanting to keep the job was not a corrupt desire. She turned her phone face down and looked at Romain instead.

"If you do it and someone from the labor board walks in, Frank gets fined," she said slowly, testing the sentence as she spoke it. "If you do it and you lose a finger, it's your hand. Either way, you're the one standing at the slicer."

"I know whose hand it is," Romain said. He was quiet then, and the quiet stretched long enough that she could hear the TV through the wall, laughter with no words attached to it. "He'll cut my hours if I say no. He's done it before. That's not theoretical, that's my bus pass."

"That's real," Maika said. "I'm not saying it isn't." And she wasn't; she had done the arithmetic too, four hours a week versus a principle, and she did not pretend the arithmetic lost. What she had decided, sitting there with the notebook between them, was narrower than a principle: the rule was not a matter of opinion, it was a fact with her signature under it, and facts did not bend to accommodate a bus pass, even a deserved one. Whether Romain should risk his hours for it, whether Frank was bluffing, whether the labor board ever actually walked into a store like Halloran's, all of that she honestly did not know.

"You could tell him the new hire flagged it," she offered. "Blame me. I already signed the sheet, he has it in the folder."

Romain almost smiled. "Throw the new girl under the bus, day one."

"Under the federal bus. It's a very sturdy bus." She slid the notebook back toward herself and closed it. He stood there a moment longer, working the pen cap on and off, then pocketed it and let himself out. She watched from the window as he crossed the street, shoulders up around his ears, phone already at his ear, thumbing out something to Frank or to Delphine or to no one.

At ten the next morning Maika was at the store anyway, filling the bread racks near the front because Saturday was her first shift and Frank had scheduled it before any of this happened. From the bread racks she could see the deli case, gleaming and empty, and the slicer behind it with its blade guard down. Romain came through the swinging door from the back room with an apron already tied, walked the length of the counter, and stopped in front of the machine. He put his hand flat on the guard, the way you'd steady something you were about to move.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
The march had thirty-two bars before the horns came in, and Clara had played them so many times that her fingers found the notes without her. She stood on the flagstones behind Mahmoud's house, clarinet still warm from the ceremony that morning, while the party spilled out around her: someone's cousin manning the grill, a cooler of sodas sweating in the sun, Damien attempting to stack three plastic cups on a fence post for reasons he refused to explain.

"You're going to play at our funeral," Mahmoud said, dropping onto the low wall beside her. "That's what that song means now. Or a graduation. Same thing, kind of."

"It's not a funeral song." She lifted the clarinet again, more out of habit than intent. "That's what I keep wondering about, actually. Why that one? Every school in the country plays it. Every single one, and nobody ever seems to ask why."

Damien abandoned the cups and produced his phone, because Damien believed every question had an answer and that the answer was ninety seconds away. He typed with his thumbs, frowning. "Pomp and Circumstance. Elgar. It says here it's a march, like a real march, military-style, part of a set of them."

Clara lowered the clarinet. "So how did it become the thing we play when teenagers in polyester gowns shuffle across a stage?"

"Wait, wait." Damien squinted at the screen. "Yale. It got played at Yale's commencement in 1905, and Elgar was there. He got an honorary doctorate of music." He looked up, delighted. "That's it. That's the whole reason. One school, over a hundred years ago, and then everybody copied them."

"Yale," Mahmoud repeated, as though tasting something. "So the most ordinary day of my life, me tripping on the stage steps in front of four hundred people, came with soundtrack supplied by an Ivy League party trick." He turned to Clara. "You played a piece of music that got its graduation job the year my great-great-grandparents were born. At Yale. For a knight."

"It's a little antiquated," Clara admitted. "The tune, I mean. It's from another century, borrowed secondhand." She was thinking of the rehearsal weeks, the band room smelling of valve oil, Ms. Nwosu conducting with a pencil because her baton had gone missing in April. Ms. Nwosu had never once explained the piece, had only said, "Again, from the top, and this time believe it means something." Clara had assumed it meant something ancient and fixed, like a law. Now it turned out it meant Yale had good taste in 1905 and everyone else had simply followed.

She told them that, and Damien laughed, but Mahmoud went quiet in the way he did when a joke brushed against something real. "My dad has this adage," he said finally. "Tradition is just peer pressure from dead people. He says it at every wedding."

"That's not fair, though," Clara said, and was a little surprised at herself. She had spent the whole spring resenting the march, resenting the gown, resenting the ritual she was performing for people who had decided its meaning long before she was born. But the fact sat differently in her now. The song wasn't a law. It was an imitation that had lasted so long it became one, and there was something almost funny about that, and something she couldn't quite allay, either, a small unease that the things she'd believed were permanent were really just habits with good posture. She tried to say some of it out loud. "It started as somebody's idea. That almost makes it better. It means somebody could have a different one."

"Nobody will," Damien said. "That's the point of traditions. They're the one thing we all agree to be unoriginal about."

The party behind them was finding its second wind; the cousin at the grill had begun, optimistically, to sing. Ms. Nwosu arrived with a plate of food and asked why Clara wasn't inside celebrating, and Clara, instead of answering, raised the clarinet and played the first eight bars of the march, slow, almost tender. Ms. Nwosu listened with her head tilted, then said, "You know, they played that at my graduation too. In Lagos. Same notes, same everything." She sounded pleased about it, and Clara found she was pleased too, though she couldn't have separated the pleasure from the strangeness of it: three continents, a century, one borrowed tune.

Mahmoud's father appeared at the door then, holding a cake and calling for everyone to come, and Mahmoud stood, brushing off his trousers, pausing with one hand on Clara's shoulder. "For the record," he said, "I didn't trip. The stage tripped me."

They went in for the cake, which turned out to say CONGRATULATIONS MAHMOUD AND CLARA AND EVERYBODY, because his father had ordered it in a hurry and told the bakery to just make it general. Damien, already cutting slices, looked up at the two of them and grinned.

"See?" he said. "Traditions have to start somewhere."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: By the JavaBeans naming convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field is usually named with 'is', like isActive().
story:
Kate had come to her grandmother's house for the quiet, and for the second reason she had not said out loud: the deadline for the Java project was Monday, and half of her team's code would not compile. Teegan had written most of it over the weekend, alone, and had named every getter differently. There was fetchScore, and grabActive, and returnStatus, and one method simply called score that returned nothing anyone could predict. Kate sat at the small desk in the back bedroom, where the afternoon light came through a curtain printed with faded birds, and opened her laptop on top of her grandmother's old Scrabble dictionary.

She had tried to raise it gently in the group chat that morning. "Should we standardize the getters?" she had typed, and Teegan's reply had been immediate and slightly bellicose, all capital letters in places capitals did not belong: "IT WORKS ON MY MACHINE." Teresa had sent a shrugging emoji and gone silent, which was Teresa's way of choosing peace over principle. So Kate was here, in a house that smelled of cardamom and old paper, doing the work of deciding whether to rewrite a teammate's code without asking, or to ask and risk the argument, or to find some third way she had not yet imagined.

The grandmother moved through the hallway with two glasses of tea and set one down beside the laptop without comment. She had been a schoolteacher for thirty-four years and had learned, she liked to say, when a student needed to be left alone. Kate pulled up the project files anyway and began to read, not to fix, just to read. The class Teegan had built held a score as a private int, an active flag as a private boolean, and then a sprawl of accessor methods with no system she could detect. It was not that the code was wrong. It was that it had no taxonomy, no shared order, and reading it felt like opening a drawer where someone had thrown forks, letters, and batteries together.

She found the answer partly by accident. Searching for how other people named these methods, she landed on a page about the JavaBeans convention and read it twice. A getter for a field named 'score' was called getScore(). A getter for a boolean field was usually named with 'is', like isActive(). She sat back. It was so small a thing, a naming pattern, and yet it would dissolve the entire mess on her screen. Every strange method Teegan had invented had a conventional twin waiting for it. She started a new branch of the project and renamed them one by one, testing after each change, watching the little green check appear in the test runner like a held breath released.

When she had finished, she called Teegan, because the third way had turned out to be this: do the work, then show it. Teegan answered on the fourth ring, voice wary. "Before you get mad," Kate said, "I found why the code was hard to read. It's not that your logic is bad. It's the names." She explained what she had found, kept it short, and then said the one sentence she had rehearsed on the walk from the bedroom to the kitchen: "By the convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field uses 'is', like isActive()." There was a long pause on the line, long enough that she could hear a television in the background.

"Okay," Teegan said at last. "That's actually kind of satisfying." Then, quieter, almost embarrassed: "I didn't know there was a rule. I thought I was supposed to be creative."

Kate thought about that for a long time after the call ended, turning her teacup in its saucer. She had spent a year of computer science believing that structure and creativity were opposites, that conventions were cages, and Teegan, apparently, had believed it even harder. But the afternoon hadproblematized that neatly: the names were only beautiful once they agreed, the way words in a sentence were only meaningful in a shared language. Whether Teegan's wild first draft or the disciplined second one was more truly hers, Kate could not say, and she suspected the honest answer was both, tangled together. Some judgments she was willing to leave unresolved, at least until Monday.

She was still at the desk when the light went amber, running the full test suite one more time to watch it pass, when her grandmother appeared in the doorway with the Scrabble dictionary under her arm. "There is a boy at the door," she said. "Teresa's brother. He says his code is broken and Teresa told him you were here."

Kate looked at the green checkmarks on her screen, all sixty-three of them, then at the door.

"Send him in," she said, and closed the laptop halfway.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: The 'Concorde fallacy' is named after the British and French governments continuing to fund the Concorde airliner after they recognized there was no longer an economic case for it.
story:
The deposit had been five hundred dollars, and it had seemed like almost nothing on the Tuesday she made it. By Saturday, sitting on a plastic chair in the dealership's showroom while a fan pushed warm air across the vending machines, Audrey counted it differently. Five hundred was the fall tuition balance at the community college, held in Ms. Cohen's office until the first of September. Five hundred was the difference between starting her course load and starting it late.

"Silvers coming in," Natan said, angling his chin toward the lot. He worked weekends moving cars between rows, and he wore the uniform the dealership made him buy, navy with the logo stitched over the pocket. He'd told her once that it cost him four hundred dollars, four shifts of pay before he'd earned a single shift in it. He hated the job, she knew that much, and yet he kept showing up.

"Then quit," she said.

"Can't. I bought the uniform."

She looked at him, then at the salesman who was walking back toward them with an equivocal answer about the transmission on the blue hatchback, something between "runs great" and "as far as we know." The salesman turned the radio down on his way past, a talk station where a populist host was telling callers that the price of everything had been fixed against them by people in offices. The salesman said something about how that guy wasn't entirely wrong either.

Audrey had a notebook in her bag, the one from Ms. Cohen's economics elective, and she had been reading it on the bus that morning not because she was studying but because the pages smelled like the class. She turned to the page she'd dog-eared in spring. "Do you know what this is called?" she asked Natan, and read him her own handwriting. "The Concorde fallacy is named after the British and French governments continuing to fund the Concorde airliner after they recognized there was no longer an economic case for it." She looked up. "They kept paying because they'd already paid."

"So?"

"So the uniform is your Concorde. You're staying because of money you already spent, not because of anything you're going to get."

Natan turned his cap backward, which was against the rules, and considered the rows of cars as if they might contradict her. "Buying the uniform doesn't absolve me of anything," he said finally. "I still hate it." But he said it slowly, like a man checking a coin against a magnet.

The salesman came back and put the keys on the desk in front of her. The blue hatchback was twelve hundred more than the gray one, and the gray one had a door that sounded like a wave breaking every time it shut, but she had five hundred dollars already sunk into the blue one and the paperwork half-drawn. That was the logic pulling at her hands as she picked up the keys. Five hundred gone if she switched. Five hundred gone if she walked. Five hundred was gone either way, and the tuition balance was not.

She thought about telling the salesman it was the Concorde fallacy too, and about how his face would go politely blank. She thought about Inaya, who had texted her that morning from the orientation at the state school: pick the thing you'd pick if the money were already spent. It had sounded so clean in the text, and here in the showroom, with the fan and the radio and Natan standing in his four-hundred-dollar shirt, it was less clean. Maybe the course load mattered less than she was letting herself believe. Maybe a car that could take her to a real job was worth a semester's delay, and Ms. Cohen, who had told them almost nothing twice, would say the numbers could argue either way.

She set the keys back on the desk and told the salesman she was going to think about it. He said the deposit was nonrefundable in a tone that was meant to close the door behind her. Natan walked her out through the rows, and at the bus stop he said he was going to talk to the manager on Monday, maybe about the parts department, maybe about leaving.

Her phone buzzed while she waited. It was Inaya again, forwarded from the department list: the fall section she'd been saving the five hundred for had been cancelled for low enrollment, moved to spring. Audrey read it twice, then a third time, and looked up in time to see the blue hatchback easing out of the lot with someone else's hand on the wheel, the salesman jogging alongside with the paperwork still flapping.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: John Lewis Gaddis's 1972 book The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947 argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, a view called post-revisionism.
story:
Mr. Krause had taped the debate question to the door of Room 114 two weeks early, as if daring anyone to walk past without reading it: Resolved that the United States bears primary responsibility for the origins of the Cold War. Mya had stopped in the hallway with her backpack half off one shoulder, oatmeal cookie still warm in her hand, and felt the particular dread of a question she could not yet hold on both sides.

She was arguing the negative, which meant she had to claim that the Soviet Union, or circumstance, or someone else carried the blame. The problem was that every source she pulled from the library cart said the same thing in different fonts. Her first draft had leaned on a historian who called American policy aggressive and uncompromising, and she had felt sturdy writing it, until Hayden read it over her shoulder at lunch and said, "This is just one guy's opinion with a lot of evidence stapled to it."

"He has archives," Mya said.

"So does the other side. Krause gave us three books. You read one."

The library smelled like radiator dust and old glue, and the afternoon light came through the tall windows in bars that reached almost to the far shelves. Mya found the second book easily, the revisionist one, and read forty pages standing up, her thumb keeping her place. It was convincing. That was the frightening part. It expatiated at length on American economic motives, on decisions made in rooms she could picture, and its confidence felt like fact. Then she read the third book, the one written first, and everything wobbled.

The third book was by John Lewis Gaddis, published in 1972, and its title ran long across the spine: The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947. She had expected another prosecutor, this time for the defense, and instead the argument refused to sit on either side of the courtroom. Gaddis argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility. She read the sentence three times, then flipped back to the introduction to make sure she was not inventing it. Neither. Sole. She copied the title into her notebook and underlined the dates, 1941 to 1947, and beside them wrote, so what do you call someone who blames both?

Lea-Maude was at the next table, ostensibly studying chemistry, actually drawing mountains in the margin of her notes. Mya slid the notebook across. "What do you call a historian who says both sides are responsible? Is there a word?"

"Post-revisionist," Lea-Maude said, without looking up. "My cousin had Krause two years ago. She said it on the phone for like an hour."

Mya wrote the word down. It looked like a label on a jar whose contents she had not yet tasted, but at least the jar existed. At home that night she spread the three books across her bed, their spines cracked at different depths like a record of hours, and tried to lay their claims side by side. Where the revisionist saw an American decision, Gaddis saw pressure that no leader could have dodged. Where the anti-revisionist saw Soviet rigidity, Gaddis conceded Western missteps. He was not saying the sides were equal, she thought, or maybe he was; she could not tell yet whether that distinction mattered, and she hated not knowing.

The debate was Thursday. On Tuesday, Mr. Krause kept her after class, not to lecture but to shuffle the essay outlines on his desk. "Your erudition is not in question," he said. "Your position is. Right now you have three authors and no Mya in the paper."

That night she cut her draft into strips, physical strips, with scissors, and taped them to her bedroom wall under two headings. Every claim went under a book's name. Then she stood on her desk chair with a marker and drew a third column down the middle, unlabeled, and began moving strips into it: the points where two historians, looking at the same evidence, agreed on what happened while disagreeing on what it meant. The agreed column filled faster than she expected. The disagreements, she noticed, were mostly about emphasis, and emphasis was a thing a person could weigh rather than solve.

In the debate itself, Hayden went first for the affirmative and was fluent and a little gratuitous with his contempt for anyone who doubted American culpability, which cost him points with the room. When Mya stood, her hands were sweating on the note cards, and she did not use half of them. She said the revisionists were right that American choices mattered, that the archival record showed real decisions by real men. She said the older school was right that Soviet behavior constrained those decisions. Then she held up Gaddis, the 1972 book, and said, "He argued that neither side could bear sole responsibility, and there is a name for that position, post-revisionism, and I think the name is less important than the method underneath it."

Mr. Krause asked from the back whether she believed it. Mya looked at the wall of taped strips in her mind, the third column, the parts that stayed stubbornly unsorted. "I believe blame is a bad unit of measurement," she said. "I believe some evidence supports more American responsibility than Gaddis allows, and I have not finished weighing it, and I would rather tell you that than pretend I have."

Hayden caught her elbow in the hallway afterward, still holding his note cards. "You could have won," he said. "You had the room."

"I know," Mya said. She held up her own cards, the bottom one blank. "I'm going to the library tonight. There's a fourth book."

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886, grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday and is considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day.
story:
The fryer exhaled its hot breath every time the basket lifted, and Charlotte had learned to count her shift in baskets rather than minutes, because minutes at the Blue Line Diner were not really minutes. They stretched and folded, an hour of dishes becoming forty minutes of pay once the manager shaved the clock, and nobody said anything, or nobody had until Thursday. That was when the schedule went up with Saturday hours cut to three and a half, and Denny, the line cook, stood in front of it with his arms crossed long enough for the whole kitchen to see him standing there.

Charlotte had taken the job because Mr. Leung, who lived two floors below her mother and ran the kitchen, had said she was reliable, and because her mother had smiled the whole walk home the day she reported it. He was the one who taught her to stack the plates so they wouldn't chip, the one who told her she could do her biology homework at the steel counter once the dinner rush thinned. Tonight the homework was still open beside the sanitizer sink, a diagram of the phylogeny of flowering plants, little branching lines showing which species shared which grandmother, and she kept returning to it between loads because the branches looked like the scheduling chart on the wall, everyone descending from the same opening shift and dividing into smaller and smaller allotments of hours.

Lorelei was on the fry station, and it was Lorelei who had taped the photocopied flyer to the break-room corkboard. It showed a crowd with fists raised and a line of block letters: MARCH ON MAY 1. STAND FOR A CONTRACT. Ashleigh had read it twice during her break and asked the question that had been sitting in Charlotte too. "Why the first of May? Like, why that day and not Labor Day or whatever?"

Charlotte dried her hands and looked it up on her phone, the screen fogging in the steam. She read slowly, partly for Ashleigh and partly for herself. The Haymarket affair, in Chicago, on May 4, 1886, had grown out of protests for an eight-hour workday. She scrolled further. Because of all that, May 1 had become International Workers' Day, the day workers marched in most of the world, even though in their own country almost nobody knew it. She said this last part out loud, and Ashleigh frowned at the flyer as if it had been keeping a secret from her on purpose.

"Those people wanted eight hours," Ashleigh said. "We don't even have that promised. We have, what, whatever he feels like."

That was the thing Charlotte could not stop turning over. There were laws, she knew, minimums for her age, rules about how late she could be kept, but the laws were floors, and the floor here was freshly mopped and slick. What Lorelei wanted was a union vote, and after that a contract, collective bargaining she called it, the workers negotiating together instead of each one begging alone. When the area manager had come through on Tuesday, he'd called the organizing doctrinaire, said Lorelei was too young to be so certain about everything, and Lorelei had laughed and said certainty was the only thing the diner had ever given her for free.

Mr. Leung had said nothing either way, which Charlotte understood to be its own kind of speech. He had cut his thumb on the mandoline that same afternoon, a clean red line that the walk-in nurse at the clinic would suture with three stitches, and before he left he had stood at the schedule chart for a long moment, touching the corner of Saturday's column the way you touch a bruise to see if it still hurts. Charlotte wanted to ask him which side he was on, but the question felt like asking a parent whether they loved you, in that both answers were true and one of them was still a wound.

The vote was Friday at nine, after close, in the break room with its mismatched chairs and the corkboard where the flyer hung. Charlotte came in with damp hair from the dish pit and sat between Ashleigh and the prep cook, and Lorelei passed out the ballots with hands that were steadier than her voice. The suspense lived in the counting, which Lorelei did out loud, slowly, each folded paper opened flat like a small wound being examined. Six for. Six against. And then the last ballot, still in the pile, and everyone in the room seemed to breathe at the same time the way the fryer breathed.

Lorelei opened it, read it, and set it face up on the table without a word.

The ballot was Mr. Leung's, and the mark beside the word YES was small and exact, the mark of a man who had taught her to stack plates so they wouldn't chip. He was standing in the doorway with his bandaged thumb, not looking at anyone, and Denny began to clap, once, twice, before the room swallowed the sound. Lorelei picked up the ballot and held it out toward Charlotte as if it were something that needed a witness.

"Call your mom," she said. "Tell her we're going to need the good coffee."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Kayla arrived at the community center early, the way she had every Tuesday for six weeks, because the piano in Room 4 was free until her lesson started and nobody bothered you if you sat quietly at it. The room smelled of floor wax and old radiators, and through the window she could see the basketball court where Kendrick was supposed to be running drills but was mostly standing near the bleachers talking to Tenley. Kayla sat down, lifted the fallboard, and began to count.

She had counted before, in a scattered way, the way you count ceiling tiles during a boring assembly. This time she wanted the actual number. She touched each white key with one finger, moving left to right, whispering the totals under her breath like a spell. Fifty-two. Then she counted the black keys, which went faster because they were smaller and she could tap them in little groups. Thirty-six. She added the two numbers on paper, because she trusted nothing she did in her head, and got eighty-eight. A standard piano, she wrote in her notebook, 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black. It felt like a fact she had earned rather than learned, the way a map you drew yourself sticks better than one you bought.

The door banged open and Tenley came in with her gym bag still on her shoulder, Kendrick behind her, both of them trailing court noise like perfume. "You're talking to the piano again," Tenley said. "It's not going to answer."

"It might. It's a very serious instrument." Kayla put her notebook face down on the bench. "Ms. Jean-Louis says I have to know the territory before I fight the war."

Kendrick dropped onto the folding chair by the window and spun it once. "That's metaphysics," he said grandly, as though he had invented the word on the spot. "Piano philosophy."

"That is not what metaphysics means," Tenley said.

"It could be. Nobody's settled it." Kendrick looked pleased with himself, which was his resting condition.

Kayla played the first four bars of the song Ms. Jean-Louis had assigned her, a simple thing with a melody like water finding its way downhill. Then she hit the F above middle C and nothing happened. Not a muted thud, not a stuck clunk. Nothing. She pressed it again, harder, the way you might knock twice on a door you suspected of being painted on.

"It's dead," she announced.

Tenley came over and pressed it herself, then pressed the neighbors, which rang out bright and ordinary. "Weird. That key's just dead."

Kayla lifted her hands and stared at the keyboard, and the thing she had written in her notebook turned over in her mind. She had counted 52 white keys. She had counted 36 black. But that had been two weeks ago, on this same piano, and she had pressed every key while counting, because the tapping was the counting. Now she wondered whether she had actually touched them all, or whether she had counted the ones she expected. She went back to the beginning, left to right, pressing each white key and listening. The dead F made no sound under her finger, and she nearly skipped it, her mouth already moving to the next number, and she had to stop herself and start the count over. Fifty-two white keys, but only 51 of them made any sound.

"You're doing the counting thing again," Kendrick said.

"I counted 52 white keys before," Kayla said slowly. "Including this one. So either I counted a key that makes no sound, which is a little bit like counting a person who never talks, or I messed up and got lucky." She cogitated on that for a second, elbow on the piano lid. "I think I counted right. It's still a key. It's just not working right now."

"So is it a key or not?" Tenley asked. "That's the real question. That's the metaphysics."

"That," Kendrick said, pointing at Tenley, "is what I said."

The door opened and Ms. Jean-Louis came in with her coffee and her folder of sheet music, took one look at the three of them hovering over the keyboard, and raised an eyebrow. Kayla explained about the dead F, and about her count, and about her notebook line. Ms. Jean-Louis listened all the way through without correcting anything, which Kayla had learned meant she had probably not said anything wrong.

"The center has a repair man who comes on Thursdays," Ms. Jean-Louis said. "Until then, we transpose. It's ancillary to the lesson, but you'll learn something from it." She set her coffee down and began flipping through the folder. "A key that doesn't sound is still a key on the page. The page is eighty-eight keys long whether or not every one of them answers you."

Kayla looked at the silent F, then at her notebook, then at Tenley, who was very obviously about to make a joke about silent letters in words. She put her hand back on the keyboard and found the melody a whole step higher, where all the keys were alive.

"Play the dead one anyway," Kendrick said from the folding chair. "Just once. For its dignity."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
Elizabeth got the folder from Mr. He on Tuesday, outside the equipment shed, and the folder had one page in it: a list of eleven names, ages nine and ten, and a note in his handwriting that said their passes die in the middle third. She read it twice. Chloe and Koraly stood behind her reading over her shoulder, which she did not mind, because they had both agreed to help run the Saturday session and neither of them had ever designed a drill in her life.

The problem showed itself the very first Saturday, faster than she expected. The girls in green bibs kept knocking the ball flat along the grass, and the girls in orange kept sticking a foot out and stopping it, and after ten minutes of this the whole exercise had collapsed into a scramble that rewarded whoever kicked hardest. Elizabeth blew the whistle and stood there with the ball under her arm, thinking that she had prepared for tiredness and for shyness, but not for this.

Mr. He had watched the first half from the touchline, arms folded, saying nothing, which was his way. When she walked over at the water break he did not offer a correction. What he said instead was, "My son plays hockey. His coach loves the saucer pass." Then he nodded at the field and left her with it.

Chloe heard the word too. "Saucer," she repeated, as if tasting it.

On Sunday Elizabeth looked it up, mostly to prove to herself that she could plan without asking an adult to hand her the answer. She found a clip, grainy, filmed from the stands, and watched one player slide the puck across the neutral zone to another. The puck rose just off the ice, no more than that, travelled flat, went over a defender's stick blade, and came down on the tape of the receiver's stick without a bounce. She watched it eleven times. On the twelfth she noticed that the pass was barely in the air at all, that the whole point was how little it rose. It lifted just enough to clear the stick and then it landed on the blade, and the play never slowed.

She sat with that for a while. Her first idea, the obvious one, was to teach the girls to loft the ball high, the way a clearance goes, but a high ball takes too long to come down and the ten-year-olds could not trap it anyway. The hockey pass was not a clearance. It was a pass that stayed low and went over the obstacle instead of around it, arriving where the receiver stood. The two games were not the same, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she did not know how far the comparison could be pushed. A ball is not a puck. Grass is not ice. But the principle, that a flat trajectory clears a low obstacle and keeps the play moving, seemed worth an hour of her Saturday.

The drill she built was simple. Koraly stood in a channel marked with two cones, orange cones for defenders who could only move their feet, never their hands or heads, and the rule was that the ball had to go over the feet and land inside a square of chalk in front of the receiver. First attempts went everywhere. One girl scooped it into the air like a goal kick and it rolled out the back. Another bashed it straight into Koraly's shin. A small girl named on the sheet as the youngest stood at the cone chewing her sleeve, and Elizabeth crouched beside her and said, "You only need to lift it a little, the height of their foot, no more," which she hoped would allay the fear without promising anything that was not true.

Then the small girl tried it. The ball hopped, hung flat for a moment like something skipping a stone across water, dropped over Koraly's outstretched boot and rolled to a stop inside the chalk square. Koraly turned around with her hands up. "Do that again," she called, and the small girl did it again, and this time two other girls were watching, and by the end of the session the channel had become the only drill anyone wanted to run.

In the last five minutes they played a small game, four against four, and it did not become beautiful. Twice the girls remembered the lifted pass when a normal one would have done, and once the ball came down on a defender's head instead of a receiver's feet, and Elizabeth had to stop play and say that the height of the obstacle was still the rule, still just the foot. But four times in ten minutes a green bib played the ball over an orange boot and a striker ran onto it, and Mr. He, packing the cones away at the far sideline, did not fold his arms.

Afterward, collecting the bibs, Chloe said that what she liked was that they had not taught the girls anything showy, only a small adjustment. Elizabeth said she was not sure it was that simple. She was still unsure whether the drill would survive a real match, where defenders jumped and slid, and she said so. Chloe shrugged and said the usual thing about how Rome was not built in a day, and Elizabeth laughed and said that was exactly the kind of bromide that got printed on the posters in the gym, the ones next to the marine biology mural with its enormous blue pelagic zone spreading across the far wall. They folded the last of the bibs together, and through the open door of the gym the painted ocean went on and on, flat and deep and out past the diving birds, and on the chalked square of the empty field the small girl was still practising alone, hopping the ball over an imaginary foot.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The molar mass of a compound is the sum of the molar masses of the atoms in its formula; for carbon dioxide it is 12.01 plus two times 16.00, or 44.01 grams per mole.
story:
The quiz was on Thursday, which meant the practice problems had to be right by Wednesday, and Alyssa's were not right. She sat at the back lab bench with her calculator balanced on a stack of handouts, the smell of vinegar still hanging in the air from first period's titration demo. Mr. Villanueva had written on the board that they would convert grams of reactant to moles of product, and he had underlined it twice, which he only did when half the class was about to lose points.

She copied her setup again from the top. Twenty-two grams of propane burned in excess oxygen; find the moles of carbon dioxide produced. Ludovik leaned over from the next station, where he was supposed to be rinsing beakers but was instead flicking water at Joey. "You look like the quiz already happened," he said.

"It happened and I failed it." She turned the calculator so he could see. "I keep getting some number that isn't any of the answer choices."

Ludovik picked up her notebook and read without touching it, the way he handled everything in a lab, as if it might be contaminated. "Your whole map is fine. Grams to moles of propane, then the ratio, then back." He tapped the page near the bottom. "It's here somewhere."

Joey came over drying his hands on his shirt, which Mr. Villanueva pretended not to see. "What are we failing?" Joey said it lightly, but he pulled a stool up beside her, and Alyssa remembered that he had failed the last quiz and had to come in at lunch, and that he never mentioned it and always laughed first at anyone's jokes, including his own, which she had started to understand was not the same as being fine.

She walked through it out loud, because saying it sometimes showed her what reading it hid. "So three moles of CO2 for every one mole of propane. That part matches the balanced equation. Then I need moles of CO2 from grams of CO2, wait, no, I need grams of CO2 first, so I go through the molar mass." She paused. "I used forty-four point zero one last night. At my grandmother's kitchen table, actually, I checked it there. Carbon is twelve point zero one."

Ludovik said, "And oxygen?"

"Sixteen." She wrote it. "Twelve point oh one plus sixteen." She looked at what she had written, twenty-eight point zero one, and then at the number forty-four point zero one sitting in last night's work, and something shifted, quiet and complete. "There are two of them." She took the calculator back. "Twelve point oh one plus two times sixteen point zero zero. That's forty-four point zero one grams per mole." She looked up. "I dropped an entire oxygen off every molecule in that kitchen."

Mr. Villanueva drifted over, hands in his pockets, the way he did when he had decided not to teach yet. "Find it?"

"She found it," Joey said, before she could, and she noticed he had copied her corrected line onto his own paper without asking, and she decided she did not mind at all.

"The compound has two oxygens in the formula," Alyssa said, mostly to herself, mostly to the page. "So the molar mass is the whole formula, not just the first atom and one of everything else." She thought of her grandmother's kitchen, the radio on, her grandmother sliding her a sliced apple without being asked, the way she always did when Alyssa spread homework across the table. Her grandmother had not gone past the sixth grade and would not have known a mole from a mole, and she had still sat there across from Alyssa for an hour, nodding at intervals, as if the nodding were ancillary to the real work of keeping the apple slices coming. It had felt like company then. It felt like something more specific now, though Alyssa could not have named it, and did not try.

She redid the problem with the right number and landed on the answer choice, and then, because the quiz would not use propane, she made up her own problem with methane, and then another with glucose, the way Ludovik practiced free throws past the point anyone made him. When she got stuck on the glucose one she asked Ludovik, who shrugged and said chemistry was an oligarchy run by people who could memorize, and she said no, actually, it was one of the only classes where the rules could not be changed by whoever talked loudest, and he considered that with the seriousness of someone reorganizing his worldview, then flicked water at her.

Joey stayed beside her the whole period. He made mistakes she caught, and she made one he caught, a transposed digit, which he pointed at without saying anything, just leaving his finger on it until she saw. Ten minutes before the bell, Mr. Villanueva collected the practice sets and told them the quiz would be one problem, one chance, clean work. Walking out, Alyssa held her notebook against her chest and thought of her grandmother's kitchen table again, the two oxygens she had lost there and found again here, and she decided she would call her tonight, not to explain it, just to say the apple helped.

"Hey," Joey said in the hallway, catching up. "Tomorrow, before, sit near me?"

"Third seat from the window," she said. "I'll save it."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Madison had claimed the sunroom table at her grandmother's house because it was the only surface in the building not already encumbered by crossword books, seed catalogues or the faint melancholic clutter of a house where one person now lived instead of two. Her laptop, three library books and a printed style guide made a small barricade around her. The paper was due Monday, and Ms. Sutton had said, twice, that she would fail anyone who treated sources as decoration rather than evidence.

The argument itself she had. Asher had sent her a message that morning: pick the claim you can actually defend, not the one that sounds smart in the first line. She had chosen the cleaner thesis, the one about migrant labour and railway expansion, and now she had a paragraph from a historian named Dr. Okafor that said exactly what she needed, only better. She read it twice, set it aside, and wrote it again in her own rhythm, her own words, her own sentence about who built the tracks and who was left off the maps. It came out well. It came out so well that she deleted the little footnote marker she had drafted at the end of the line, because the sentence was hers now, wasn't it? She had not copied a single phrase.

Her grandmother drifted through with a watering can and paused at the table. "Footnotes," she said, tapping the style guide. "Your grandfather wrote a whole book of those. People thought they were the boring part. He said they were where you found out who a man had been listening to." She moved on toward the ferns, and Madison stared at the sentence she had made, feeling something in her chest tighten the way it did before a race.

She thought of October, of Karter leaning across the lab bench with his plagiarized physics conclusion, three lines lifted whole from a website, the meeting with Ms. Sutton, the probation letter that seemed to debilitate him for weeks, his shoulders folding in at lunch when anyone mentioned the class. Everyone had agreed that was clear-cut. He had copied. But what Madison had done was different, she told herself; she had transformed it, the way her grandmother transformed cuttings into new plants. She closed the laptop and went to help water the ferns, and the two of them worked in silence except for the sound of the can and the tick of the old radiator.

"You've gone quiet," her grandmother said at last, not looking up. "That's your grandfather's quiet. He got it before a chapter he was afraid of."

"It's nothing. A paper."

"Mm." The old woman straightened, pressing a hand to her back. "There's a box of his in the closet if you want it. The notes, I mean. The actual notes." She said it lightly, but her eyes stayed on Madison a moment longer than the words required, and Madison understood that she was being offered something more than a box.

In the closet, under folded cardigans, she found the box and opened it on her grandmother's bed. There were the published books, and there, in a thick folder, the drafts. In one draft a paragraph appeared underlined, and in the margin, in her grandfather's slanted hand: "Okafor, p. 212. Reworded entirely. Still his." Madison sat down slowly on the edge of the bed. The same historian. The same author, decades earlier, and her grandfather had reworded him too, and had decided, in ink, that the idea still belonged to Dr. Okafor even when the words did not. She read the line three times, as if it might rearrange itself into something more forgiving. It did not. Somewhere between his sentence and hers, she understood that plagiarism covered using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording, and that what she had deleted was not housekeeping but theft, however prettily disguised.

She carried the folder back to the sunroom and worked fast now, no longer pausing to admire her own phrasing. She restored the footnote, added the bibliography entry, formatted it the way the style guide demanded, checking twice because her hands were unsteady. When Asher messaged again asking if she was surviving, she typed back, "Barely. My grandfather just saved me from myself via medium," and then deleted "via medium" as too much, which was a lesson in itself.

At the kitchen table that evening, her grandmother ladled soup and asked, without ceremony, whether the paper had gone well. Madison said it had, mostly, though there was a part she still wasn't sure of: whether she would have caught it on her own, without the box, without the lucky accident of the same author on the same shelf. "Maybe not tonight," her grandmother said, spooning more soup into her bowl. "But you'd have caught it eventually. The ones who don't catch it are the ones who never open the closet." Madison looked at the folder sitting between the salt and the bread, and pulled it closer to her plate.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly 3 million volts per metre, which limits how strong a field can be across an air gap.
story:
Taylor sat on the top platform of the climbing frame with a worksheet folded against her knee, because the picnic tables were all in direct sun and the wood there had been hot enough at noon to feel like a stove. She was eighteen and had until Thursday to learn what she had not learned all semester: how to find the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates. The playground was empty except for a man raking sand near the swings and, further off, Tess, who came across the grass carrying two slushies and wearing the expression of someone who had opinions she was saving.

"You skipped the review," Tess said, handing her the blue one.

"I didn't skip it. I sat in the back and copied the board and understood nothing." Taylor smoothed the worksheet on her knee. The problem gave her two plates, a potential difference of 6,000 volts, a separation of 2 millimetres, and asked for the field at the midpoint. The formula was the part she could manage: field equals voltage divided by distance. What she could not manage was why the formula was allowed to be true, why a number on paper could be trusted to describe anything in a room.

She did the arithmetic out loud, because saying it made it more real than writing it. Six thousand volts across two millimetres. Two millimetres was two thousandths of a metre. Six thousand divided by two thousandths was three million. Three million volts per metre, and the field was uniform between parallel plates, so the midpoint got the same value as everywhere else. "Three million volts per metre," she said, and tasted the size of it and found she had no taste for it at all. Numbers like that were the reason she had stopped doing physics homework in April.

Tess leaned on the railing and looked at the sand below, where the rake was dragging its slow lines. "Three million," she said. "That's the ceiling."

"What ceiling."

"The air breaks down at about three million volts per metre. Sea-level pressure, dry air. Any stronger than that across a gap and it sparks. Mr. Zhou did a demo with two spheres and the whole class jumped." She drank some of her slushie. "So you're sitting exactly on the line."

Taylor looked at her answer. The paper had not changed, but the playground had, a little. The gap between the plates in her problem was a gap of air, ordinary air, the same air moving through the chain-link fence and stirring the sand in the crawler pit. If the field was at the ceiling, the air was at its ceiling too, and the difference between a stable answer and a spark was nothing she could see on the page. She thought of the question the way Mr. Zhou put questions, which was never "compute" but "could you build it." Whether a number was buildable was a different question from whether it was computable, and she had spent the spring treating them as the same thing.

"That means my number isn't just an answer," she said. "It's a design limit. If the exam says four million, the answer isn't four million, it's four million and then lightning."

"Then lightning," Tess agreed.

Mr. Zhou was crossing the parking lot with a bag of groceries, and Taylor called out to him before she decided whether she wanted to. He came over and stood in the shade of the platform, a small mercurial man whose moods the whole class tracked the way sailors track weather, and he asked to see the sheet. He read it without touching it, hands staying on the grocery bag.

"Where did the number come from?" he said.

"Dividing. Six thousand by two millimetres."

"And where did the ceiling come from?"

Taylor hesitated. "Tess. From your demo." She had wanted to say she had reasoned it out herself, and the honesty cost something small. He nodded once, the way he nodded at data, and said, "Then check it," and walked on toward his car, and she understood that being told to check it was the enfranchising part, the part where the problem belonged to her instead of to the curriculum. She checked it. Three million volts per metre, sea level, dry air. The demo had been in April, the month she stopped working, so it had happened without her.

She tried the next problem, which raised the voltage to 9,000 across the same gap, and wrote 4.5 million volts per metre, and then, in the margin, where no one would grade it, she wrote "sparks." She did not know yet whether that was an answer or a complaint. The worksheet wanted a number; the world wanted a machine that did not catch fire. Somewhere between those two wants was the actual physics, and she suspected it stayed uncertain on purpose, the way the rake man's lines in the sand stayed uncertain, each one drawn straight and each one about to be smoothed by children or weather or the next pass of the rake.

Tess had gone to the swings and was pumping high enough that the chains went slack at the top. Taylor folded the worksheet into her pocket, where the corners dug into her hip, and climbed down. The bars were warm under her palms and smelled of sun-baked metal. At the bottom she looked at the two-metre gap between the climbing frame and the slide, tried to imagine three million volts sitting across it, failed completely, and found the failure useful: it told her exactly where her imagination ended and the arithmetic had to begin. She walked over to the swings.

"If I get the last one right," she said, "you owe me the red slushie next time."

"Four and a half million," Tess said, dragging her feet to stop. "You don't get it right. It sparks."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Nicolas had shared the video before first period, standing in the corridor with his thumb already moving, because the footage was so awful it felt wrong not to pass it on: a drowned parking garage, cars floating nose-down, a caption claiming it was the highway collapse from last Tuesday's storm. Two hundred people he didn't know had liked it within an hour. Now, in fourth period, the school computer lab smelled of warm plastic and the radiator ticking under the window, and Mr. Wanjiru was writing something on the board that Nicolas couldn't read from the back row.

"Today you're going to break a photograph," Mr. Wanjiru said, which was the kind of thing he said when he meant something ordinary. He had posted a single image on the class page: a shark swimming down a flooded street. "Before the end of the period, tell me where this picture is actually from and when. That's all. You'll need a tool, and I'm not going to give it to you."

Around Nicolas, keyboards began their rattling. Tristen leaned back in his chair with the particular posture of a boy who intended to wait for someone else to do the work. "It's from the hurricane," he said. "Everyone posted it. My grandma sent it to the whole family with about forty exclamation marks."

"So did mine," Nicolas said, and something in his stomach shifted, small and cold. His grandfather had forwarded the parking garage video to him directly, with a message that read, stay safe at school, thinking of you. Nicolas had forwarded it onward. He hadn't checked anything. He hadn't even thought about checking.

Zaina, two seats over, said without looking up, "My cousin told me about this. Reverse image search. Google added it, like, ages ago." She turned her screen slightly toward them. "It's called search by image. You upload the picture or paste its link and it finds where else it shows up on the web. Old dates, other places, everything."

Nicolas pulled up the shark photo, copied its link, and pasted it into the image search. The results loaded in a stutter. There it was: the same shark, the same grey street, but the pages were from years ago, some from 2011 when the tool itself was new, others rehashing it after every flood since. The shark had been swimming down that street for more than a decade. It was practically in symbiosis with disaster reporting, one feeding the other, neither true. Tristen came to stand behind him and let out a long breath through his teeth.

They tried it with other images, a competition forming without anyone declaring it. Zaina found that a "last week" factory fire was from three years earlier. Tristen, obdurate for a while, kept insisting his examples were different until his own screenshot of soldiers on a bridge turned out to be from a movie set, and he went quiet, then laughed, then said, "Okay. Okay, I take it back." Nicolas opened his messages, found his grandfather's forward, and pasted the parking garage footage's key frame into the search, expecting the same satisfying collapse.

The results came up half-loaded and then, oddly, clean. News outlets, dated last Tuesday. Local reporters at the scene. The garage was real, the flooding was real, the caption had been true. Nicolas sat there while the radiator ticked and Tristen argued with Zaina about whether the shark was more or less embarrassing than the bridge, and he tried to understand why he felt cheated of something. He had wanted the tool to make him smarter than the crowd, and instead it had made him slower than his own thumb. It would be easy to impute some virtue to the delay, to say that checking was always the moral act, but he wasn't sure. If he had waited an hour before sharing, some classmate might not have known about a real flood in time to call a parent. The tool didn't tell you what to do with what it found. It only told you when the picture was taken.

The bell was minutes away. Mr. Wanjiru wandered the rows, unhurried, looking at screens rather than faces. Nicolas opened a new message to his grandfather, typed "that video was real, by the way," then deleted it, then typed again. What he wanted to say was that he'd learned to check, and that checking had left him less certain about the checking, and that both of those things seemed true at once. Too much for a text. He attached the search results instead, the four oldest pages the engine had found, and pressed send. Tristen peered over. "What did your grandpa say?" Nicolas shrugged. "Nothing yet."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Most US and Canadian jurisdictions use graduated licensing, in which new drivers move from a learner's permit to a provisional license with restrictions before a full license.
story:
Nevaeh adjusted the seat three times before she touched the key, once for distance, once for height, once for distance again, and her mother watched all of it from the passenger seat without comment, which was worse than comment. The parking lot of the community centre was empty except for a man loading folding chairs into a hatchback and, at the far curb, Azaan, who had texted her an hour ago with the words "big news, come get me after" and then nothing further.

"Mirror, signal, shoulder check," her mother said. "Then we go."

The car lurched, stopped, lurched again, and crept out of the lot at a speed that made the folding-chair man pause and look. Nevaeh kept her hands at ten and two the way the handbook demanded, though the handbook, she was beginning to suspect, had been written by someone who had never actually been seventeen and desperate. When they pulled up beside Azaan, he leaned down to the window before she had fully stopped, and she braked harder than she meant to, forestalling whatever he was about to do with the door handle.

"I got my permit," he said. He held it up. The photo made him look like a suspect in a documentary. "Three hours ago. Get in, we're going to the lake."

"I'm in the middle of a lesson," Nevaeh said. "And I have a permit too. As of this morning."

"So you can drive. Perfect. I'll navigate."

Her mother had turned in her seat with the expression of someone assembling bad news in order of delivery. "He can't come with us," she said to Azaan, not unkindly. "Not with Nevaeh driving."

Azaan's face did something complicated. "You have a permit," he said slowly, as though she had failed to understand her own paperwork. "That means you can drive."

"That means I can drive with a licensed adult in the car," Nevaeh said, and even as she said it she heard the shape of the thing she had not read carefully enough, the fine print she had skimmed at the counter while the clerk slid the card across. She took out her phone, thumbed through to the state page her mother had bookmarked in a rare moment of sagacious foresight, and read it aloud in the flat voice she used for homework. "It's graduated. You start with a learner's permit. Then you get a provisional license, which still has restrictions. Only after that comes the full license."

"Restrictions like what?"

She scrolled. "Like how many passengers, and what hours. It depends." She didn't say on what, because she hadn't got that far, and she wasn't going to pretend she had.

Azaan sat down on the curb with the permit still in his hand, and for a moment Nevaeh thought he might actually be heartbroken, which struck her as absurd until she remembered that she had spent most of June imagining this exact afternoon differently too, windows down, three people, a destination chosen on impulse. He had clearly spent his whole morning imagining it. "So I can't drive anyone around," he said. "Not my cousins, not anybody. I just wait."

"You just wait," her mother confirmed, and then, because she was not a monster, "Get in the back seat and ride along. You can be the first person she's ever driven somewhere."

He got in. Nevaeh pulled out of the lot for the second time, and this time it was smoother, or at least less eventful, and Azaan narrated from behind them like a disappointed sports commentator. "She's braking like her dad," he reported at the second stop sign. "That has to be phenotype. It's in the blood."

"It's day one," Nevaeh said, but she was laughing, and her mother was laughing, and the laughter loosened something in her shoulders that had been tight since the parking lot. She had spent the morning thinking of the permit as a door swinging open, and Azaan had spent his morning thinking the same, and both of them had been wrong in the same direction, which felt like its own kind of company.

They drove the long loop past the school, past the soccer field where Mr. Siddiqui was setting out cones for the evening clinic, past the turn that would eventually lead to the lake. At the light by the pharmacy, Nevaeh said, mostly to the windshield, "I keep wanting to say it's unfair. But it isn't, exactly. It's slow, and those are different things."

"Easy for you to say," Azaan said. "You're the one driving."

"I'm the one driving with my mom in the car and a passenger limit and a curfew I haven't even read yet. I just got done being mad about it, and I'm already halfway to not being mad, and I don't fully trust either feeling." The light turned green. She checked the mirror, signalled, and turned, and the turn was clean, the best thing she had done all day.

"So what do we do all summer?" Azaan asked.

Her mother said, "You ride with people who love you and wait," and Nevaeh, watching the road open ahead of them, long and straight and entirely legal at twenty-two miles an hour, said, "Get in line. I'm driving to the lake when I'm allowed to, and you're the second person I'm picking up."

"Who's first?"

She signalled, checked her shoulder, and changed lanes. "Ask me when I have the provisional."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: US employers withhold 6.2 percent of an employee's wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit.
story:
Tristan told himself he was the kind of person who noticed things, and for sixteen years the claim had mostly held. He noticed that Ms. Ivanova, owner of Kessler's Hardware, kept the register keys on a carabiner clipped to her belt loop, and that she hired him on the spot when he reorganized the loose bolt bins without being asked. He noticed his own certainty, arriving for his first shift, that he would be good at this. What he did not notice, yet, was how quickly a version of yourself could calcify into something you had to keep defending.

The job came with a deadline. Inventory had to be finished before the store closed Sunday night, because the supplier's truck came Monday at seven and Ms. Ivanova refused to order what she could not count. So Tristan spent his first two weeks hauling paint cans off shelves, tallying screw packets, learning the smell of fertilizer and the exact squeak of the back door. Bryson, who worked the register on weekends, told him the work would ruin his summer. Rania said any job where you weren't handling french fries was a victory. Tristan said the money was for a bus pass and a laptop that actually booted, and he had done the math on how many hours that would take.

Then the first paycheck came, in a thin envelope Ms. Ivanova handed over at closing, and the math stopped working.

He sat on the loading dock after hours with the stub under the streetlight, running the numbers on his phone. Forty hours at eleven dollars an hour. Four hundred forty dollars. The check said considerably less, and the difference wasn't the small dent he'd braced for. He counted the stub's deductions twice, then a third time, and each pass he skipped past a line he didn't understand, because the number next to it looked wrong and wrong numbers made him want to look away. He decided, standing up, brushing dust off his jeans, that Ms. Ivanova had shorted him. It was easier to believe that than to believe in a line item he couldn't read.

He did not say anything that night. He rehearsed it instead, which is to say he lied to himself in draft form: he would be calm, factual, adult about it. Bryson, when Tristan texted him, replied "she seems cool though" with three question marks, which Tristan chose to read as agreement. Rania, at school the next day, was the detractor his plan didn't need. "You're sure it's not taxes?" she said. "Everyone's check is smaller than they think."

"Forty times eleven is four hundred forty," Tristan said. "I know arithmetic. I reorganized her bolt bins."

"That's not the same as knowing payroll," Rania said, but he was already walking toward the parking lot, where his ride was idling, and he told himself her doubt was just the usual noise.

Saturday morning, with the Sunday inventory deadline hanging over the store like weather, he asked to speak with Ms. Ivanova in the back office, among the filing cabinets and the calendar with the supplier's logo. He laid the check and the stub on her desk and said, evenly, that the amount didn't match his hours. He waited for her face to close, for the argument, for maybe the end of his first job two weeks in.

She picked up the stub and turned it toward him, tapping one line with a paint-stained finger. "Social Security," she said. "Six point two percent of your wages, withheld. Every employer does it." Tristan looked at the number he'd been avoiding, multiplied it out on his phone, and watched it come to exactly 6.2 percent of his gross pay. Not a shorting, then. Not theft. Just a piece of his money going somewhere he hadn't planned for, taken before the check was ever cut. He felt the accusation calcify-dissolve in his chest, leaving something more like embarrassment, though he wouldn't have used that word.

"Does it stop?" he asked. "Or do they take it forever?"

"Up to a yearly wage limit," she said. "Past that, no. Not something you'll worry about this summer." She slid the stub back across the desk. "You're still on for tonight and tomorrow. Truck comes Monday."

He worked the rest of Saturday with the numbers running quietly underneath, recalculating the laptop, recalculating the bus pass, recalculating how many Saturdays he had left before school. He still didn't love giving up the 6.2 percent; he liked the idea of choosing where his money went, and he understood, dimly, that the withholding was a bet on a version of himself decades away, one he couldn't picture. Maybe that was fair and maybe it wasn't. Rania would have said it was fine, Bryson would have said the whole system was profligate, and Tristan, hauling the last of the paint cans toward the count sheet, held both opinions at once and committed to neither.

At closing, Ms. Ivanova unclipped the register keys and paused at the back door. "Next paycheck," she said, "read the stub before you read the check."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The porch fan turned overhead, and Layla spread her notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with the good spoons her grandmother was burnishing for Eid. The presentation was at nine the next morning. Ms. Navarro had paired the seniors with the tenth-grade advisory groups, and Layla's group had drawn the short straw of topics: consent, contraception, and how to actually get tested at a clinic. Two months of the semester had gone toward preparing them, which meant there was no version of tomorrow where she could fake it.

"You're the tenth grader," Layla told Farah, who had biked over with a sleeve of crackers and her feet already up on a chair. "Ask me anything they'd ask. Be rude about it."

"I'm always rude about it." Farah popped a cracker. Behind them, at the stove, Layla's grandmother stirred cardamom into tea and said nothing, though the spoon slowed whenever the word consent crossed the table, which Layla noticed and did not name.

Layla started with consent, because everything else sat downstream of it. She had decided on the plainest phrasing she could hold onto under pressure: it has to be freely given, it can be taken back, and silence isn't it. Farah tested her, dragging out a situation where one person keeps asking until the other stops arguing, and Layla held the line. "If you have to wear them down, you don't have it," she said. Farah wrote that on a napkin, which was how Layla knew it had landed.

Then the hard part. Layla held up the laminated chart Ms. Navarro had printed, the one with every method ranked by effectiveness, and made herself say the number aloud before she lost her nerve. "So this one surprises people. With typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy. Mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time." Farah sat up, crackers forgotten. "Thirteen? The box makes it sound bulletproof." Layla tapped the row above it. "The box is talking about perfect use. Typical use is real people on real Tuesdays." She let that sit, then gave them the takeaway Ms. Navarro wanted them to carry: a second method alongside condoms, and where the county clinic fit in. Free, confidential, no parent signature needed after sixteen, results by text in under a week.

"Would you actually go, though?" Farah asked, quieter now. "You, personally, walk in?"

Layla looked at the doorframe where her grandmother had gone still, listening the way she listened to the radio, without turning toward it. All fall Layla had been circling the same tension: the curriculum wanted her to say get tested, like it was a trip to the library, while half the girls she knew would rather not know. And the other half of her, the part that had watched her cousin marry at twenty with no one explaining anything to her, wanted the information shouted. She didn't think both halves were wrong. She thought they were both true at once, and that her job tomorrow was to hold the door open without pushing anyone through it.

"You go with someone," Layla said finally. "That's the actual answer. You book the appointment together, you sit in the waiting room together, and it stops being a thing you're doing alone in secret." She wrote that in the margin of her script, in pen, underlined twice. "Maely already said she'd come with me if I ever needed it. I'd go with her. That's part of the lesson I keep forgetting to say out loud."

Her grandmother set a cup of tea beside Farah's elbow and one beside Layla's, and paused with her hand still on Layla's shoulder. In the cabinet behind her, on the shelf where she kept the stones Layla had collected as a child, the little metamorphic chunk from the creek sat between two cups, its bands pressed and folded by whatever had held it under pressure long ago. Layla had liked it as a kid because it looked like it had survived something.

"Run the last part," Farah said, mouth full. "The clinic part, from the top. You stumble on the address."

"I do not stumble."

"You absolutely stumble."

"One-twenty Riverside, walk-ins on Wednesdays," Layla said, faster than she needed to, and Farah threw a cracker at her, and her grandmother laughed into her tea.

"Again," Farah said, straightening the chart. "And this time say the thirteen thing like you're not scared of it."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
Dylan had been in Oakley's basement perhaps two hundred times, but never with a deadline. The county programming contest closed submissions at nine, and it was already half past six, and the three of them sat cross-legged on the carpet beneath a shelf of anachronistic VHS tapes that Oakley's father refused to throw out, laptops glowing on the folding table between them.

"It times out," Angela said, turning her screen around. "Nine seconds. The limit's two."

Dylan leaned over. Their program read a list of two hundred thousand numbers, then, for each name in a long file of queries, walked the whole list from the beginning looking for a match. He could picture it, a finger dragging down a page, line by line, starting again at the top every single time. How many times had they made the computer do that tonight?

"Linear search," Oakley said, with the gravity of a doctor naming a condition. "It's called linear search. You check every item one by one."

"There's a faster thing," Dylan said. He had read about it that week, half understanding it, the way you half understand a rumor. "Binary search.
