You cut the list in half, then in half again, until you find what you want." He grabbed a paper napkin and a pen. "But it only works if the list is sorted."

Angela frowned. "So we sort it first."

Oakley was already typing, but Dylan stopped him with a hand on his shoulder. "Wait. How long does sorting take?"

They tested it. On the full list, their quicksort ran in just under three seconds. Three seconds, and then every search after that was nearly instant, a rabbit dive through narrowing halves. Dylan watched the numbers fall away, half then half then half, and felt something click into place, the same click he got when a French verb finally conjugated itself in his mouth.

"Here's the thing," he said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "Sorting costs more than one search through the list. So if we only had to search once, sorting first would actually be slower. We'd pay three seconds to save one. Sorting pays off only if we search the same list over and over."

"Which we do," Angela said, pointing at the query file. "Thousands of times. Look."

But Dylan was already worrying at the other edge of it, because a decision like this felt like something that needed adjudicating rather than just announcing, and he was the one who had argued for waiting. "If there were only one query," he said, "we'd be idiots to sort. We'd be paying three seconds to avoid one. It's only because the same data gets searched again and again that the sort is worth it." He looked between them. "So the question isn't which is faster. It's how many times we're going to search."

"Four thousand and twelve," Oakley said, having counted. "I counted."

They rewrote it together. Dylan wrote the binary search itself, and twice he got the boundaries wrong, once sending the search spinning off into an infinite loop, and Angela caught it because she was the only one still patient enough to print the list on paper and trace it with her finger, like an epicure reading a menu slowly enough to actually taste it. By eight forty the program ran the full input in just over a second. They submitted at eight fifty-one, and Oakley collapsed backward onto the carpet with his arms out, a martyr to computer science.

The confirmation email arrived while Dylan was capting the last of the flat cola. "Accepted," Angela read. "And, oh. There's a note. Sample input for judging, they say."

Dylan scrolled to it. The judging data, the file their program would actually be graded against, contained one query. One. A single name to find, once, in a list of two hundred thousand.

He sat very still, doing the arithmetic he already knew how to do. If they had known that from the start, the whole elegant machine they had built tonight, the sort, the halving, the napkin diagram with its arrows, would have been the slower choice. The plain dumb finger-drag down the page would have won.

"So we built the fast thing," Oakley said from the floor, "for the one night the slow thing was better."

"Nobody tell the judges," Angela said, and closed the laptop.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: NOT EXISTS is another way to find customers with no orders: it keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row.
story:
The computer lab smelled of warm plastic and the lemon wipes Mr. Lau used on the keyboards at lunch, and Tyler had been staring at the same half-finished query for twenty minutes. The assignment was simple to say out loud and apparently impossible to type: two tables, customers and orders, and a question. Which customers ordered nothing? He had the customers, all four hundred of them, and he had the orders, a swirling mess of rows, and no idea how to ask one table about the people missing from another.

"Your face looks like the blue screen," said Rose, dropping into the chair beside him with her bag still on her shoulder. She leaned over, read his screen, and made a small humming noise, the kind she reserved for other people's code. "You're doing the join backwards. You want to keep the customers who don't match."

"Thank you, oracle," Tyler said. "Now say that again in a way that helps."

Micheal arrived with two juice boxes, set one on Tyler's keyboard like an offering, and cracked the other with a sound like a small firework. "Mr. Lau said there's more than one way. He said that like it was a riddle. I hate when he does the riddle voice."

"He does the riddle voice because he enjoys it," Rose said. "It's practically metonymy. The riddle voice stands in for the whole man. You see Mr. Lau, you hear a riddle."

Tyler typed while they argued, feeling his way along the LEFT JOIN. He joined customers to orders, kept every row on the left, and then asked for the ones where the order column came back empty. It felt almost like cheating: don't match anything, then keep the leftovers. When he ran it, the database gave him back a tidy list of eleven names. People who had signed up and never bought a thing. He sat back as if he'd invented fire.

"You look smug," Micheal said.

"I feel smug. Smug is the natural state of a person with eleven correct rows."

Rose, though, was already on the classroom whiteboard wiki, scrolling with one finger. "Here. Look at this other one. There's a thing called NOT EXISTS. It keeps each customer for whom a subquery finds no matching order row." She turned the screen so both boys could see. Tyler read it twice. A subquery: a question inside a question, a little net cast into the orders table for each customer, one at a time.

"That can't give the same answer," he said. "It looks completely different. Mine keeps leftovers. That one checks everybody, one at a time."

"So run it," Micheal said, in the reasonable tone of a boy who wanted to drink his juice and watch someone else panic. "If they disagree, one of them is lying and we get drama."

Tyler typed it carefully, the way his grandmother did passwords. Each customer, and inside the parentheses, the orders table searched for a matching row. He ran both queries side by side and the screen returned two lists. Same eleven names. Same order, even, as though the database had no imagination whatsoever. He stared at them for a long moment, juice box forgotten and sweating gently onto the desk. Two ways of thinking about absence. One said, throw everything on the table and sweep off the matches. The other said, go person by person and ask, does even one order exist for you? The lists were identical, and yet they felt different in his hands, like two maps of the same city drawn from opposite directions.

"I like mine better," Micheal said, pointing at the LEFT JOIN, "but I couldn't tell you why, so my opinion is worthless."

"That's the most honest thing you've said all week," Rose said. "Mine's better for understanding what's being asked. His is better for feeling clever."

Tyler pulled his notebook over and wrote both versions down, drew an arrow between them, and added a question mark, because he couldn't yet say whether the two approaches were truly the same underneath or merely agreed on this one answer, the way two witnesses can describe the same accident in words that never overlap. Mr. Lau drifted past on his after-school rounds and looked at the question mark for a second and a half, said nothing, and kept walking, which was somehow worse than the riddle voice.

"He saw the arrow," Micheal whispered. "He saw the arrow and walked away."

"Then the arrow stays," Tyler said, and underlined the question mark twice.

At home that night he tried a third way that failed spectacularly, returned four hundred customers, and taught him that ANDs are not free. He emailed the screenshot to Rose with the subject line "my database is doctrinaire." Her reply came in under a minute: a picture of her own screen, both queries side by side, and one line beneath them: "still eleven, still uncertain, see you tomorrow." He screenshotted that too, and set it as his wallpaper, and went down to dinner grinning at nothing anyone else could see.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor is generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities.
story:
The gym's front desk smelled of chlorine and lemon cleaner, and Levi had worked there long enough to stop noticing either. Saturday mornings he restocked the towel bin, answered the phone, and slid laminated waiver forms across the counter to new members. Each form had a signature line at the bottom, above a block of text in small print that listed terms and conditions, assumption of risk, and a release of liability. Members signed without reading it. Levi watched them do it, dozens of them, pen scratching, initials in the little boxes.

Hussain, who worked the desk on weekends beside him, had been reading the employee handbook in the back room during his breaks. "You know you can get the staff discount on a membership," he said one morning, tapping the page. "Half price. You just fill out the contract like anyone else."

Levi had wanted a membership since September, when the cross-country coach started renting lane time at the pool and Levi discovered he was the slowest swimmer on a team of runners. He took the form home and read it that night. It was four pages. There was a clause about liability, a clause about cancellation terms, a clause about consent to a credit check. On the last page, in bold, it said the member must be eighteen or older, or have a parent or guardian co-sign.

His mother worked nights at the hospital and slept days, and asking her meant leaving the form on the kitchen counter with a sticky note, which felt, though he could not have said why, like asking her to take responsibility for something he had already decided. He put the form in his backpack and brought it to work instead.

At the desk he asked Hussain, quietly, whether the rule mattered. "It's a contract," Hussain said. "You can't just sign it. It wouldn't be, like, real." He said the last word with a shrug, as though he suspected realness was negotiable.

That afternoon a boy from Levi's grade, Danick, came in to cancel his membership. He'd signed up in July, before his birthday, and his mother had never co-signed. Danick had read the fine print, all of it, which Levi found out when Danick slid the contract across the counter and pointed to a highlighted line. "I looked it up," Danick said. "A contract made by a minor is voidable by the minor. In most of the US. That's common law. Except for necessities." He said the last part flatly, quoting something. "So I can void this thing, and they have to give me my deposit back."

Levi photocopied the page Danick had highlighted, ran the cancellation through the system, and gave him the deposit in cash from the drawer. Afterward he stood in the back room with the photocopy, reading the line again. If a minor could void a contract, then his own signature on the membership form would mean nothing the gym could rely on. And if it meant nothing, then requiring his mother's signature wasn't the gym being bureaucratic. It was the gym wanting a contract that could not be walked away from, and only an adult could give it that.

Ms. Nielsen, the manager, came through on her rounds at four, checking the towel count. She had a florid way of talking about the gym, calling it "a family" and the members "our community," which Levi had long since learned to hear as background. He asked her, anyway, why the co-sign rule existed.

"Because a seventeen-year-old's signature doesn't bind," she said. "That's just the law. We need somebody on the hook." She counted towels while she talked. "You've been sensitized to the paperwork, I can tell. You notice things now." She stacked the last bundle and went back out front.

Levi thought about Danick, who had used the rule to get free of something, and about Hussain, who had called a contract real as though reality were the point. Both of them were right in some way Levi could not fully line up. The rule that let Danick escape was the same rule that kept Levi waiting for his mother's handwriting. It protected him and it stopped him, and he could not separate those into two different rules.

He took the form out of his backpack during his break and set it on the table in the back room. At the top he wrote his name where it said member, and at the bottom, on the signature line, he wrote his name again, full and careful, knowing it was a signature that bound no one but himself. Then he folded the form, put it in his pocket, and clocked back in.

On Monday morning the form lay on the kitchen counter with a pen on top of it. His mother had not signed it yet. There was a sticky note in her handwriting next to the signature line that said, "We'll talk Tuesday." Levi ate his cereal, put his dishes in the sink, and left for school with the form still sitting there, the pen uncapped beside it.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
The afternoon light came through the tall windows of the art classroom and fell across Sarah's canvas in a long pale bar, which was the only thing about the painting she liked. She had been working on a landscape of the lake near her grandmother's house for two weeks, and the horizon still sat stubbornly in the middle of the canvas, exactly where she had first drawn it, because she could not decide whether moving it was honest or merely obedient.

"Put the horizon a third of the way down," Jadon said from the next easel. He said it the way he said most things, as though he were reading from a manual no one else had been given. "It's the rule of thirds. Everything looks better off-center."

Sarah set her brush across the rim of her water jar. "Who made that rule?"

Jadon shrugged, which she had learned was his way of retreating with dignity. Jordyn, who was gluing bottle caps into a mosaic at the back table, looked up with interest, because a question like that in this room usually meant Sarah was about to argue with someone, and Jordyn considered that better entertainment than the radio.

"I mean it," Sarah said. "Somebody had to write it down first. Somebody stood in front of a painting and said, one third, there, that's the law." She was only partly joking. She had spent the whole semester half in love with composition and half suspicious of it, the way you can be suspicious of a language you speak fluently anyway. Her grandmother, who had painted for sixty years and never taken a class, put horizons wherever she pleased, and her paintings were better than anything Sarah had made, which was either an argument against rules or an argument for having earned the right to ignore them.

Mr. Friedman was at his desk grading sketchbooks, and he did not look up, though she could tell from the stillness of his pen that he was listening. He had a policy of not answering questions like hers, a policy she found both admirable and infuriating. So she took out her phone and typed the phrase in, hunched over the screen so it would look like research and not defiance.

The result surprised her into sitting down on the stool. "It's a guy," she said. "It was first written down by John Thomas Smith, in 1797. In a book called Remarks on Rural Scenery." She read it twice to be sure. "So it's not a law. It's an observation one man made about a couple of paintings more than two hundred years ago, and everybody's been repeating it ever since."

"That doesn't make it wrong," Jadon said.

"No," she agreed. "That's the annoying part."

She sat with it while the others kept working. She was not, by nature, someone who could introspect quietly for long; her thoughts tended to come out of her mouth on their way to being thoughts. But for a moment she held it privately: the rule was arbitrary and the rule worked, and both of those things were true, and the fact that John Thomas Smith had been just a man with an opinion in 1797 made the rule smaller and somehow more usable, the way an island is easier to visit than a continent. Or, she thought, turning the phrase over, the way an archipelago is easier to cross one piece at a time than a single vast landmass would be. She almost said this out loud and then didn't, because Jordyn was already walking over to look at the screen, being her usual loquacious self, narrating the discovery back to the room as though Sarah had excavated it from a tomb.

"Eighteenth century," Jordyn said. "That's so old. He probably wore a wig."

"He probably looked at rural scenery and had opinions," Sarah said. "Like I'm having opinions right now."

She picked up the brush again. The horizon was still in the middle of the canvas. Below it was the lake, which she had painted as a flat band of grey-blue, and above it a sky she had spent three days on, layered and luminous, better than the water by far. If she moved the horizon up, the lake would shrink and the sky would swell, and the painting would be more conventionally balanced and less hers. If she moved it down, she would be giving the water more room than it had earned.

Mr. Friedman passed behind her on his way to the supply closet and paused. "Smith was describing what he saw in other painters' work," he said, and then, as if remembering his own policy, added nothing further and went on to the closet.

Sarah looked at the canvas for a long moment. Then she turned it around on the easel, picked up the palette knife, and scraped the horizon line out entirely, leaving a smudge where the division had been, lake bleeding into sky, sky into lake. It was the kind of thing her grandmother would have done and the kind of thing the boy in 1797 would probably have hated.

"You're going to fail the composition unit," Jadon said.

"Probably," Sarah said, and began mixing a grey the color of weather that hasn't decided yet.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Chinese New Year's Eve reunion dinner, fish is traditionally served because the word for fish, 'yu', sounds like the word for surplus or abundance.
story:
Alice had the notebook open on the counter beside the steaming rice cooker, and the page said, in her mother's handwriting, "fish, cannot be left off." Below it her own handwriting said, "why not." She had been asking that question since Tuesday, and the answer had so far arrived only as a look, the kind her mother gave when something was so obvious it embarrassed them both.

"You could just make it," said Emilio, who had come over supposedly to help but was currently eating the practice dumplings straight off the tray. "Steam a fish, braise a fish, nobody's going to fail you."

"It's not a test," Alice said. "It's dinner. My grandmother's coming, my uncle's flying in from Toronto, and my mom has done it every single year, and this year she's sitting down and I'm running it." She turned the notebook toward him. "It's a whole sequence. The order of dishes matters. There's a thing with the fish where you're supposed to leave some on the plate."

"Why would you leave fish on a plate on purpose?"

"I don't know yet. That's the part that's making me insane."

Emilio waved a dumpling at her. "Text Ireland. Ireland knows everything and will tell you at length."

So Alice texted, and the reply came in three installments, the last of which she read aloud while Emilio listened with his mouth full. "okay so I asked my grandma," Ireland had written, "and she laughed at me and then made me repeat it back twice. at the reunion dinner on new year's eve, fish is served because the word for fish, yu, sounds like the word for surplus or abundance. that's it. that's the whole thing. she says you leave some fish uneaten so the surplus is still there at the end, like you have so much you can't even finish it. also she says stop texting during dinner."

Alice set the phone down on the counter, screen still lit. "It's a pun," she said. "The entire menu is holding up a pun."

"It's a good pun," Emilio said. "Puns you can eat are the highest form."

She laughed, and then she didn't, because something was assembling itself in her head that she couldn't quite say out loud yet. She had spent a week approaching the dinner like a project, timelines and temperatures, as though the ceremony were a set of tasks she could optimize, a kind of cheerful solipsism in which the meal existed only as her performance of it. But the fish was not a task. It was a sentence being spoken, slowly, by everyone at the table at once, and her job was less to perform it than to make sure the sentence could still get said.

Her mother drifted into the kitchen for tea and glanced at the notebook. "You have the fish down."

"Steamed, with ginger and scallion," Alice said. "And I'm going to leave some on the plate on purpose. For the yu."

Her mother's mug stopped halfway to her mouth. "Who told you?"

"Ireland's grandmother. Through Ireland. Through me."

"I was going to explain it during dinner," her mother said, and there was something in her voice Alice hadn't expected, a small loss in it, as though a gift had been unwrapped early. Alice felt the shape of the choice before she felt its content: she could let her mother explain it, hand the ceremony back over the table, or she could carry it herself and let her mother sit, for once, in the guest's chair of her own kitchen.

"You can still explain it," Alice said. "I'll ask, in front of everyone. Like I don't know. I'll say, Mom, why is there still fish on the plate."

"Then it would be a little bit a lie."

"A little bit," Alice agreed. "A yu-sized lie."

Her mother laughed then, the real laugh, and Alice wrote at the bottom of the page, "mom explains fish, alice asks." Then, because the rehearsal could not be all philosophy, she opened the oven and discovered that her second attempt at the niangao had desiccated into something like a floor tile. Emilio picked up a corner of it, tapped it against the counter twice, and set it back down with ceremony.

"It's surplus," he said solemnly. "You have so much cake you can't even finish it."

"Get out of my kitchen," Alice said, and swept the crumbs into her palm, already recalculating the steam time for the third and final attempt, because tomorrow the fish would arrive whole and gleaming from the market and there would be no practice run for that.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Jake woke on election morning with the uneasy feeling that he had forgotten something, the way you feel a set of keys in a pocket that turns out to be empty. He found the voter information card on his desk, addressed to his mother, and beside it his own notebook with the riding names copied out during a boring shift at the grocery store. His own name was nowhere. He searched his email, his junk folder, the drawer where the household mail collected: nothing. Eighteen for four months, and apparently he had assumed that being old enough would transmute him automatically into a registered voter, the way some people assume turning eighteen makes you an adult.

He called Loik first, because Loik had voted in the provincial election the year before and acted like a veteran of everything. "I never got a card," Jake said. "Did you get a card?"

"I got a card. But my cousin didn't, and he voted anyway." There was the sound of Loik eating cereal on the other end. "An eligible voter who's not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day. That's the whole thing. Bring ID."

"You're sure?"

"I'm sure he voted. I'm sure he complained about the lineup. Beyond that, ask someone who isn't me."

Jake's mother had already left for work, so he crossed the hall and knocked on Ms. Rivera's door, because she had lived in the building since before the balconies were glassed in and considered it her office to know things. She came out wiping her hands on a towel. "I don't want to bother you," he said, "but if you never registered, can you still vote today?"

"At the polling station," she said. "That's how I did it the first time, back when I thought I had to be some kind of civic dilettante with a file of paperwork. You just show up where you're assigned. Take your passport and something with your address. A bill, a lease, your mother's mail with your name on it if that's what you have." She looked at him more closely. "You're nervous."

"A little. Everyone in my group chat is arguing about strategic voting and I don't even know if I'll get through the door."

"Then go find out. Standing in a lineup is not the hardest part of anything."

He went back inside and assembled his documents on the kitchen table with the care of a man packing for a border crossing: passport, bank statement, the notebook with the riding names. He texted Anas, who was in his first year at university and had opinions the way other people had breathing. Anas wrote back a paragraph about how first-time voters were statistically unreliable, and then, a minute later, a second message: "Actually forget that. My dad never voted until he was forty and he says it's the thing he regrets like a congenital condition, something you're born carrying. Go. I'll meet you there after my class."

The polling place was a school gym two blocks over, the same gym where Jake had failed his grade ten basketball tryouts, which struck him as a minor joke the universe was telling quietly to itself. A woman at a table near the door looked up his address, printed something, slid a form across, and pointed him to another table. Nobody made a speech. Nobody seemed to find him remarkable. The pencil behind his ear felt absurd and then, suddenly, functional.

Behind the cardboard screen he looked at the ballot for a long moment. He had read the platforms, argued with Loik, argued with Anas, changed his mind twice about the local candidate and once about the party. He still held two loyalties in his head at the same time: the one that said vote for the future you want, and the one that said vote for the outcome you can live with. They had not merged into a single clean conviction and he suspected they never would, and that this was probably what everyone else was also carrying into booths across the country, pretending it was resolve.

He marked the ballot, folded it, and fed it into the box. Outside, the October light was doing something generous with the maples along the fence. His phone buzzed: Anas, standing at the corner with his backpack on one shoulder, holding two coffees. "So it worked," Anas said. "The registering thing."

"Worked fine. Took ten minutes." Jake took the coffee. "You still think first-time voters are unreliable?"

Anas looked at the gym doors, at the people filing in with their coats and their strollers. "I think I'm changing my mind about a couple of things this week," he said. "Come on, you can tell me who ruined the country over there, and I'll tell you you're wrong."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for $250 million.
story:
The notification lit her phone at 11:42 on a Tuesday, and by midnight the group chat had forty-one messages. It had started innocently: Bria posted a link to a Washington Post story about warehouse workers with a line of fire emojis and "everyone read this before current events tomorrow." Zara answered within a minute with a different link, a blog post arguing the story was softer than it should have been, and then the chat stopped being about the article and started being about whether the article could be trusted at all.

Abigail sat cross-legged on her bed with her laptop open, the Post story on the left half of the screen and the chat on the right. She had been the one to suggest the topic for their seminar, working conditions at fulfillment centers, and now she felt responsible for the mess it was becoming. Bria wanted the story to be a weapon. Zara wanted it to be a scandal. Nobody, as far as Abigail could tell, wanted to know what was actually true.

"it's a hit piece," Bria typed. "look at the byline, this guy has been on Amazon for months."
"or it's a cover-up," Zara typed back. "they buried it on a tuesday."
"you two know it can be neither, right," Abigail typed, and then deleted it, because that was the kind of line that made people angry without making anything better. Instead she opened a new tab and typed two words into the search bar: Washington Post owner.

The answer came up faster than she expected. She read the sentence three times. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013, for 250 million dollars. She did the arithmetic against the cost of her family's house and then stopped, because the comparison was absurd and she knew it, and because the number itself wasn't the point. The point was that a man who owned one of the largest companies in the world also owned the newspaper writing about that company.

She pasted the link into the chat. "found this," she wrote. "bezos bought the post in 2013. two hundred fifty million."

The typing bubbles appeared, disappeared, appeared. Then Zara: "EXACTLY. so of course they go easy."
Then Bria, slower: "wait, but the story is still critical of amazon. it's literally about worker injuries."
"that's the trick," Zara answered. "enough criticism to look real, not enough to matter."

Abigail set the phone face-down on the quilt and looked at the ceiling. The problem was that Zara's argument explained everything, which was the same problem as Bria's. Both of them were impervious to evidence, each theory shaped so that any new fact could be absorbed without changing it. A critical story proved the cover-up was subtle; a harsh story proved the truth was undeniable. She wanted something less satisfying, which was a guess she could actually test.

She picked the phone back up. "i'm not saying either of you is wrong. i'm saying we can't know from one article."
"so we say the media is bought and call it a day," Zara wrote.
"or we compare," Abigail wrote. "zara find a story on the same topic from a paper bezos doesn't own. bria, find the post's toughest amazon piece ever. if there's a pattern we can see it. if there isn't, we can't, and we say that."

There was a long pause, long enough that she thought they had both gone to sleep. Then Bria sent a link to a Post investigation from two years earlier, the kind with charts, and the single word "ok." Zara sent a Reuter's piece, then "fine. but i still think ownership matters." Below it she added, "mr. goldberg is going to love this. he's been on us about sourcing all semester."

The next afternoon the four of them sat in Mr. Goldberg's room during the free period, laptops open, arguing about the apportionment of blame: how much of a story's slant could be assigned to an owner, how much to an editor, how much to the ordinary fear of a reporter who wanted to keep her job. Mr. Goldberg mostly listened, which was his way, and asked questions at the worst possible moments, which was also his way. When Zara laid out the ownership argument, the 2013 sale, the 250 million, the Graham family handing over the paper, he nodded and said, "And what would count as evidence against that?" Zara had no answer, and Abigail watched her face close and then, slowly, not close.

"That's the part I hate," Bria said, gathering the cables into her bag. "We did all this work and the honest conclusion is 'maybe.'"

The hallway outside was loud, the end-of-day crowd undulating past the doorway in a slow wave, everyone headed somewhere warmer. Zara stood in the middle of it, not moving. "I'm still presenting the ownership angle," she said. "I want people to know who owns what they read."

"And I'll present the part where the Post still ran the hard story," Bria said. "Somebody has to."

Abigail zipped her bag shut, the sound very loud in the small room. "Then I'll do the middle part," she said. "The part where we don't know."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between large parallel plates the field is nearly uniform, so away from the edges a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point midway between them.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and solder, and by nine in the morning every folding table along the perimeter held its small claim to order: a volcano baking soda had ruined overnight, a turbine turning slowly under a desk lamp, a row of bean seedlings taped to a poster board like evidence. Maxime set his two aluminum plates on their acrylic stand, twelve centimeters apart, connected the positive terminal to one plate and the negative to the other, and switched on the battery pack. His exhibit was meant to be a map. He had promised, in his abstract, to compute the electric field strength at nine points between the plates and draw the field the way a weather map draws wind.

He had spent the drive to the school deciding how to do it. The plan relied on the voltmeter, on the difference in potential between the plates, on dividing by distance. He had done the midpoint first, at six centimeters from either plate, and gotten a number he liked, a clean four hundred volts per meter. Then he had started the second point, three centimeters from the positive plate, and become absorbed in a problem that seemed to him a matter of rigor: the probe had to be exactly three centimeters from one plate, which meant exactly nine from the other, and his ruler had a bent corner, so he borrowed a caliper from his father's toolbox without asking, and he was still squinting at the caliper when Tess arrived with her coffee and her own poster rolled under her arm.

Tess wanted the judges to stop at her table long enough to hear the second sentence of her explanation. Her project, a study of whether bean plants lean toward a weak electrical source, had produced results she herself called equivocal: some seedlings bent, some did not, and the ones that bent had bent in more than one direction. She had rehearsed a way of framing this, uncertainty as honesty, but she needed someone to practice on, and Maxime was the nearest person who would hold still. "Tell me if this sounds defensive," she said, and delivered her opening, and Maxime, still measuring, said "mm" at what he hoped were the right intervals.

The trouble was that his numbers refused to differ. At three centimeters from the positive plate he read the same four hundred volts per meter he had read at the middle. He checked the probe, checked the battery, wrote the number down, moved the probe to two centimeters, and read four hundred again. He measured to each plate twice with the caliper, certain he had misplaced something, and the distances were correct, and the field strength did not care about them. He sat back on the folding chair. Somewhere behind him a judge was asking the volcano kid about viscosity.

"Are you getting bad data?" Tess asked, watching his face rather than his hands.

"The opposite," Maxime said. "That's the problem. It's the same everywhere." He tapped his notebook. "Midway, it's four hundred. Near the plate, it's four hundred. I measured the distance to each plate like it mattered, and it doesn't."

Tess came around the table and looked at the nine empty cells in his data table, the grid he had planned to fill with nine distinct values. She said, slowly, that her grandmother had a word for the origins of a thing, its provenance, and would ask where an object had come from before deciding what it was worth; and that Maxime had spent an hour on the provenance of a number that turned out to have no history at all, the same number no matter where he measured it. Maxime laughed, a short, surprised sound. He drew a single arrow through the middle of his map, then more arrows, evenly spaced, all the same length, all pointing from the positive plate to the negative one.

"Large plates," he said, mostly to himself. "Away from the edges, a point near one plate has the same field strength as a point in the middle. It's uniform." He said the word uniform the way you say a word you have just met. He thought about all the measuring he had not needed to do, and about how a person could subsume a morning of careful work under one sentence, and how the sentence felt like both a loss and a gift.

When the judges came by, an older man with a clipboard and a woman in a Ms. Dela Cruz lanyard, Maxime explained his map, and the man asked why he had not reported values at different positions to show the variation. Maxime said there was no variation to show, near the plate or midway, away from the edges, and that the caliper in his bag had been the least necessary object he had brought. Ms. Dela Cruz wrote something down, and her pen did not stop in a way that told him anything.

Tess, at the next table, got her two sentences out, and then a third, and the woman with the clipboard stepped closer to her seedlings. Maxime watched his friend gesture toward the bent stems, the ones that leaned and the ones that stood straight, and he understood that she had wanted this more than she had admitted on the drive over. He picked up the caliper, closed it with a small click, and slid it into the side pocket of his bag, where it lay against the notebook with eight empty cells and one good number.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
The line at the community centre moved in short shuffles, and Aiden counted eleven people ahead of him, then lost count when a woman with a stroller rejoined from the washroom. He had turned eighteen in October, six weeks before the election, and had carried the voter card in his wallet ever since, the way other boys carried receipts they meant to deal with later. Beside him, Emaan was reading the sample ballot on the wall with the concentration of someone defusing something.

"You're staring," Aiden said.

"I'm deciding. There's a difference."

Outside, visible through the glass doors, Maximus stood beside a folding table stacked with pamphlets for the school board candidate his uncle was managing. When he spotted them through the glass, he waved both arms, then held up a single pamphlet like evidence in a trial.

Aiden's mother had opinions about that candidate. On Tuesday she'd called him a carpetbagger, and on Thursday, when the newspaper ran its endorsement of the incumbent, she'd read aloud from a scathing column and paused at the good parts to look at Aiden over her glasses. His father took the opposite view, more quietly, over dishes: that the incumbent had done nothing worth hating, and that nothing was underrated.

Neither of them had told him what to do, exactly. That was the trouble with parents who respected your autonomy. They cajoled by atmosphere instead of instruction, and you left the kitchen with their arguments in your head, wearing your own name.

Flashback: he was eleven, standing in this same community centre hallway while his mother voted in a by-election. She'd gone behind the cardboard screen and he'd tried to follow, and she'd held the curtain aside and said, no, this part is just mine. He'd stood in the corridor studying a poster about recycling until she came out, and the mystery of it had bothered him for days, that a thing could be so important and so private at once.

The line advanced. At the desk, Mr. Luo, who had coached Aiden's soccer team for three seasons and now appeared to referee elections, checked his name against a list, crossed it off with a ruler-straight stroke, and handed him a folded ballot inside a plain envelope.

"Why the envelope?" Aiden asked. "Nobody here even knows who I am."

"Doesn't matter," Mr. Luo said. "Nobody sees how you mark it. Nobody's allowed to."

Aiden held the ballot, folded and light as a letter. "Was it always like that?"

Emaan leaned in from behind him. "There's a name for it. Australian ballot. We did it in civics last month."

"Why Australian?"

"Because the Australian colonies introduced it. Tasmania and Victoria, in 1856." Emaan said it the way he recited chemistry equations, flat and certain, and then added, in his own voice, "Before that I guess you just voted out loud somewhere. Which sounds like a cafeteria."

Aiden carried the folded ballot toward the row of screens, and the fact arranged itself in his mind alongside everything else. Tasmania and Victoria, 1856. A design old enough that his great-grandparents had voted inside it, and his mother behind her curtain, and now him. It was a strange kind of inheritance, one that didn't tell you what to choose, only that the choosing belonged to you. His physics teacher would have called the alternative entropy, every preference dissolving into noise the moment it left your mouth.

Behind the screen, he unfolded the ballot and found the school board race near the bottom. He thought of Maximus's uncle's pamphlets, his mother's column, his father's defense of nothing. He could still hear all three, and he noticed he didn't particularly want any of them silenced. They could argue in his head as long as they liked, as long as they stayed on their side of the cardboard.

He marked the circle beside the incumbent's name, then looked at it for a long moment, the pencil still in his hand, and the mark already drying.

He refolded the ballot, slid it into the envelope, and stepped out. Emaan was waiting by the boxes, and through the glass doors Maximus was holding up his pamphlet again, eyebrows raised in a question.

Aiden walked out, took the pamphlet, and folded it into his wallet, next to the voter card he no longer needed. "You want coffee?" he said. "I'm buying."

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state.
story:
The strawberries had gone soft in the west field, and Ava's grandfather wanted them picked before the rain he could smell in the wind but that the app on her phone said would hold off until morning. She bent between the rows with Zayan and Deegan, who had come out for the weekend partly to help and partly because Ms. Schneider had assigned their class a debate for Monday: whether countries can ever actually agree on an environmental problem. Ava had drawn the affirmative. Deegan, insufferably pleased about it, had drawn the negative.

"So your whole case is hope," Deegan said, dropping a bruised berry into the compost bucket. "That's not evidence, that's a mood."

"My case is history," Ava said. "Which you'd know if you'd opened the packet." She had read it twice on the bus out here, in the diesel smell, past the subdivisions swallowing the old orchards and the signs offering five-acre lots. Somewhere in the packet, between the graphs and the treaties that failed, there had been one paragraph about ozone, and she had folded the corner down.

The rain came early anyway, a thin drizzle that turned the dirt to paste on their forearms. Her grandfather called them in, and they sat in the barn with the door half open, watching water sheet off the tin roof while the hired hand, a man from Guatemala whose visa paperwork had stalled twice this year, mucked the stalls and said nothing. Ava's grandfather talked instead: about the bank, about the price of grain, about how the co-op wanted them all to switch to a cover-crop program that would cost money now and pay back in soil nobody could guarantee. "Everything's connected," he said, not as wisdom but as complaint. "The bank's connected to the weather, the weather's connected to some treaty I'll never read."

In the barn office, with its mildewed ledger books and a wall calendar from 1998, Ava found the debate packet in her backpack and read the folded paragraph aloud. "The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state."

Zayan looked up from his phone. "Every single one?"

"That's what it says."

"Every country on earth agreed," Deegan said slowly, "to stop making the stuff that was burning a hole in the sky, and they actually did it." He sounded betrayed by his own side of the debate.

The lugubrious light of the raining afternoon made everything in the office look older than it was, and Ava sat with the paragraph, testing it against what she knew. Her grandfather was right that systems braided together: the chemical company that made the refrigerant, the farmer who bought the cooler it ran in, the bank that financed both, the workers who came north because the climate had shifted the coffee back home, the treaty that sat above all of it like weather. Deegan was right too that the hole in the ozone had been simple in a way the warming world was not; you could name one class of chemicals and ban them. Still, they had banned them. Every state, one signature. It had happened in the world, on this planet, in her father's lifetime.

Ms. Schneider arrived at five to drop off a crate of jars her sister wanted, and found the three of them still arguing in the office. She wouldn't referee, though. "I'm not doing your cross-examination for you," she said, and handed Ava a jar of last summer's tomatoes, and drove off through the puddles.

Later, in the kitchen, Ava taped two pages to the refrigerator door: Deegan's list of failed summits and collapsed targets on the left, the Montreal paragraph on the right, and between them she wrote a single sentence her grandmother read over her shoulder: "Agreement is possible when the cost of not agreeing is visible, and impossible when it isn't, and I don't know which one this is." Her grandmother said it sounded like something you could defend. Deegan, drying dishes, said it sounded like losing. Zayan said it sounded like the farm.

After dinner the rain stopped and the hired hand drove his truck out the long lane, tailpipe ticking, and Ava walked to the west field in the wet dark. The remaining berries would split by morning, her grandfather had said, and it would be their fault, his fault, the weather's fault, nobody's fault. She knelt in the mud and kept picking anyway, filling the flat one row at a time, culpability and stubbornness sutured together in her shoulders, until the moon came up over the tree line and she could see, at the far edge of the field, the lights of the new subdivision going on, house by house, all at once.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
The toast ended and Carter's grandfather set down his glass and said, almost to the napkin, "You've got more diploma than I ever did." Around the long table the aunts went quiet in that performative way they had, and Carter's mother said, "Dad, that's not the point tonight," which meant it was exactly the point. Carter was eighteen as of that morning, and in three days he was supposed to stand in a polyester gown while a man he'd never met read his name.

He followed his grandfather out to the porch, where the old man always retreated after the second glass of wine. The screen door clapped shut behind them. "What do you mean, more diploma?" Carter asked.

"I mean I never finished high school. I was in the Pacific when I should've been a senior." His grandfather settled into the white chair with the broken arm. "But I got my GED after. The tests were created in 1942, for service members and veterans like me who hadn't finished school, so we could show we had the skills anyway. High-school-level skills." He said it lightly, the way he recited the years of his medals.

Carter sat on the railing. He had spent four years treating his own education as a series of gates he was being shoved through, and here was a man who had fought for the equivalent of the key. Something in him, some opinion he'd been carrying around like a hall pass, began to destabilize. "So you took a test and that was it?"

"That was it. And then the GI Bill, and then your mother." His grandfather looked at him sideways. "You're not excited about Friday. Your grandmother sees it."

"It's not that." But it was partly that. He had spent the spring arguing with Kole, who called graduation ceremonies empty theater, the state certifying its own product, and with Adelaide, who had cried when the college decisions came and called the ceremony the one ritual we have left. Carter had bounced between them like a spectator at a match he'd bought tickets to by accident. Ms. Taylor, his history teacher, had told him in April that people who can't hold two ideas at once become ideologues, and he'd liked the sentence so much he'd never tested it.

"Kole says the diploma's just paper," he said now. "That the whole thing's for the parents."

"Kole's never been shot at for a piece of paper." His grandfather drained the glass. "Or maybe he's right. I honestly don't know. I wanted mine because I'd been told I was finished, and I wasn't finished. Maybe you want yours because you've been told you're starting. Different hunger, same paper."

Carter turned that over. Inside, his mother called that dinner was being served and that they had a schedule, since half the family had flights in the morning and the cake had to happen by nine. Deadlines even here, he thought; the whole family ran on them. He went in, but he carried the conversation with him like something warm in his coat pocket.

At the table, Adelaide had arrived late from her own family's dinner and pulled a chair in beside him, still in her good shoes. "Kole's not coming," she said. "He texted that ceremonies are a virulent strain of sentimentalism. His word. Virulent."

"That's a strong word for a caps and gowns."

"It's a strong word for a flu." She stole a roll off his plate. "Are you glad? Be honest."

He looked down the table at his grandfather telling the aunts some story with his hands, at his mother cutting the cake early because of the flights, at the paper announcement with his name letterpressed in the center because his mother had ordered it in March without asking. "I think I'm glad," he said. "Not because of what it proves. I honestly don't know what it proves. But he wanted one and couldn't have it, and I get to just... stand there." It wasn't the position he'd expected to arrive at, and he could feel where it stayed soft, the parts Kole might still be right about. He let it stay soft.

The clock said nine, and the candles got lit anyway, one small flame for a boy who was, as of midnight, starting to figure out what he'd been carrying. His grandfather leaned over and tapped his fork against a glass.

"To the graduate," he said. "And to 1942."

Carter laughed, stood up, and raised his water glass to the ceiling fan.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: A 2008 trial in Norway found that young female soccer players aged 13 to 17 who did the FIFA 11+ warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall.
story:
The clipboard was Maria's idea, and already she suspected it was a mistake. She stood at the edge of the park's gravel pitch with seven of her teammates sprawled in the shade of the only tree, and every one of them watched her hold it like a prop in a play about someone more organized than she was. Saturday was the first session she had ever planned alone. The old captain had graduated in June, and the coach had said, in the tone of a person handing over a debt, "You're the one who actually cares," which was either a compliment or a sentence.

"Okay," she said. "So the season is ten weeks. I split it into blocks." She turned the clipboard around so they could see the grid she had drawn the night before, squares filled with her careful printing. Hard days on Tuesdays and Thursdays, skills on Wednesday, and Sundays circled and left deliberately blank.

"Blank means what?" Caiden asked, lifting her head off Colin's jacket.

"Rest. Actual rest. Whole day off."

Colin groaned the way people groan when they are seventeen and cannot imagine being tired for more than an hour. "We're only playing Sundays, though. Why does everyone need a whole day of nothing?"

Maria had asked herself the same question at two in the morning, sitting on her bedroom floor with a printout of an article she'd found after her hamstring scare in the spring. She had been out five weeks that spring, and the inactivity had been worse than the pain, a long melancholic stretch of watching from the bench while the team reshaped itself into something that no longer needed her. When she came back she started reading everything she could find about injury prevention, partly for the team and mostly, though she didn't say this out loud, so it would never happen to her again.

"Because that's how the training actually works," she said. "You break down on the hard days and build back on the rest ones. If we go hard every day we just break down and stay broken." She didn't entirely understand the physiology, and she said so plainly. "I can't explain the science part. I just know the plan."

Caiden sat up, which Maria had learned to read as a sign of actual interest rather than politeness. "So what's this bit at the start of every session? 'FIFA 11+,' it says. Twenty minutes."

"Ten minutes, maybe fifteen." Maria tapped the grid. "It's a structured warm-up. Running drills, some strength stuff, balance. You do it before every single session, exactly in order." And then, because she had promised herself she would say the number instead of hedging, she gave it to them straight. "There was a trial in Norway in 2008. Young female players, thirteen to seventeen, who did the FIFA 11+ had about a third fewer injuries overall."

"A third," Colin repeated, as if testing whether the number would hold weight.

"A third fewer. That's the whole finding, that's all I've got." She let it sit. The gravel glittered in the heat, and somewhere across the park a father was teaching a much smaller girl to trap a ball, bending down to demonstrate with his hands cupped soft.

The silence went on longer than she wanted, and she could feel the plan slipping toward the fate of every plan made by someone their age, which was polite agreement followed by quiet abandonment. So she did the thing she'd decided she would do if talking failed. "Fine. Try it once. Right now, full sequence, and if it's stupid we cut it and you get to say you told me so for the rest of the season."

They did it in the flattest corner of the pitch, and it was, at first, exactly as stupid as promised. Colin fell out of the single-leg stance twice and laughed so hard at himself that Caiden started laughing too, and then Maria was laughing and losing her own balance, and the exercise that had enraptured her in a quiet library became something else entirely out here, something messier and warmer and harder to control. By the last drill they were sweating and the mood had shifted without anyone announcing it. They had done the whole thing, together, all seven.

Afterward Caiden walked back with her to the tree, carrying the clipboard Maria had forgotten on the grass. "Sundays off is going to kill Colin," she said. "He'll show up anyway."

"Then we'll deal with that when it happens." Maria took the clipboard and looked at the grid again, at the empty circles she had drawn with such certainty, and understood that the plan was already not quite the plan anymore, that it would keep changing every week in ways she couldn't foresee, and that she was going to keep making it anyway.

Caiden pointed at the last square of the page. "What's after week ten?"

"Nothing. That's the end of the season." Maria studied the small blank space beyond her grid and then closed the clipboard over it. "Come on, we're running it back before they get bored."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The wings arrived during the second quarter, and Sarah slid the basket to the middle of the table so everyone could reach, which was a gesture she regretted immediately because her little brother took the biggest one. The big screen above the bar showed the Olympic basketball final, court glare flattening every face at Marisol's into the same blue. Her father had claimed the booth nearest the screen. Magaly sat across from Sarah, wearing her flag colors as a scarf, and Diego sat at the end, narrating the game in a lugubrious voice whenever his team turned the ball over, as if each turnover were a personal bereavement.

"Sarah," Magaly said, pointing her fork at the screen, "during the break they'll show the rings again. Look for your flag in them. It's a thing my abuela does."

Sarah had been half watching the little animated rings in the corner of the broadcast all afternoon, five interlocked circles drifting across the screen like jewelry. She liked the game fine. What she wanted, more honestly, was for the meal to end without her father starting his peroration about how sports had gone soft, a speech he amortized across every family dinner by delivering it in installments, so that no single evening bore the full cost. "Look for my flag in them how?" she asked.

"Like, your colors. My abuela says the rings hold everybody's flag in them somehow. Every country." Magaly shrugged, as if to disclaim responsibility for grandmothers.

Sarah considered this with the skepticism she had recently begun applying to all inherited wisdom, a habit she was still calibrating. Her flag was green and gold with a blue field, and she looked at the rings, blue and yellow and black and green and red, floating on the white of the screen, and thought: well, green, yes, and blue, and there was the white around them, if white counted, which felt like cheating.

The quarter ended. On the screen the rings spun in their slow promotional orbit, and Sarah pulled up the restaurant's terrible wifi and searched. The answer came back fast, from an archive page with a photograph of a serious Frenchman in a mustache. Pierre de Coubertin had designed the five rings in 1913, and he had chosen the colors, the blue, yellow, black, green and red, together with the white background, so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them. She read it twice. She looked up at the screen, where the rings spun again, and felt the small vertigo of a thing that had been decoration all afternoon becoming an argument.

"Every flag at the time," she said aloud. "In 1913. He picked the colors so every flag that existed then had at least one of them, including the white background."

"See," Magaly said, vindicated, scarf shimmering. "Abuela."

"Your abuela undersold it," Sarah said. "She left out the Frenchman."

Diego groaned at a turnover and then, catching the tail of the conversation, said, "Wait, white counts? White's not a color, white is a fridge."

"White is a background and it counts," Sarah said. "It's load bearing."

Her father leaned in, and she braced for the installment, but what he said was, "So if a country made a flag after 1913 with, say, only orange in it, the rings wouldn't cover it." Sarah confirmed this was exactly the kind of loophole the design left open, and he nodded slowly, as if auditing it, and stole one of her fries, which in his language was approval. Diego proposed that they test every flag they could remember against the rings, and for the rest of the halftime show the table deteriorated into flag trivia, Magaly defending a lavender stripe on some micronation's banner that Diego had invented entirely, the two of them appealing to Sarah as referee, which she refused on grounds of jurisdiction.

The third quarter started. Sarah found she was watching differently now, checking every cutaway to the crowd for flags, matching them against the five colors like a customs officer. The design was a hundred years old and it was doing its work right now, silently, on a screen above a basket of wing bones. It was a promise that had been made before anyone at the table was born, and it held, mostly, and where it didn't hold, the gap was small enough that people like Diego would argue about whether white was a fridge. She still wasn't sure whether she found that moving or merely tidy, and she decided she was allowed not to decide yet, that undecided was itself a seat at the table.

Magaly undid her scarf and tied it around Sarah's neck, backwards, so the colors hung down her back where she couldn't see them. "There," she said. "Now you're in the rings and you don't even know it."

Sarah reached behind her head and did not pull it off. On the screen, someone sank a shot from the corner, and Diego stood up so fast his chair tipped, and the whole booth erupted, and the rings floated on above them all, holding every flag they had ever been asked to hold, spinning slowly, keeping their old word.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: New York Times v. Sullivan (1964) held that a public official suing for libel must prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false or made with reckless disregard for truth.
story:
The porch screen at her grandmother's house had a torn corner, and every few minutes a moth tested it, found the gap, and was gone. Victoria spread her notes across the card table anyway, because the porch was cooler than the kitchen and quieter than her house, where her little brothers argued about everything except the things worth arguing about. She had drawn a line down the center of a legal pad. On the left she had written the newspaper. On the right, the mayor.

The case for the mock court had arrived in Mr. Yang's email that morning: a fictional mayor sued a fictional paper over an error, and each student had to argue both sides, five minutes each, before a panel of seniors. Hugo had already texted her twice, certain the paper should win, certain the error was small and the mayor was thin-skinned. Victoria wanted to beat Hugo, honestly, but more than that she wanted the version of herself who could hold both sides at once without dropping one. She was eighteen and about to leave for a college where, her father kept saying, everyone would be smarter than her, and she wanted to arrive already knowing how to think rather than merely what.

The trouble was the 1964 case she'd found on her grandmother's ancient desktop, the screen still warm from solitaire. She copied the holding onto a card and read it aloud to the porch. "New York Times v. Sullivan. A public official suing for libel has to prove actual malice." Her grandmother, shelling peas two chairs over, looked up. "That doesn't sound malicious to me. Sounds like law talk." Victoria read on. Actual malice meant the statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth.

"Wait," she said, mostly to the moth. "It's not about whether the paper was mean. It's about what the paper knew." She flipped the legal pad over and started again. If she argued for the mayor, she could not simply show the story was wrong, which it was, the number misreported, the meeting misdescribed. She had to prove the reporter knew, or didn't care enough to check. If she argued for the paper, she could admit the error freely and still exculpate it, as long as the mistake came from honest confusion rather than recklessness. The same fact cut both ways depending on what she could show about the reporter's state of mind, which was almost impossible to show, which was, she suspected, the entire point of the rule.

Her grandmother set down the bowl of peas and watched her write. "Your grandfather used to do that," she said. "He'd take the side he disagreed with just to test it. Drove his brother crazy at Thanksgiving." She wanted, Victoria understood slowly, to be part of the work and not just adjacent to it, and so Victoria read her the hypothetical aloud, and the old woman frowned and said, "Well, did the reporter call anybody before he printed it?" It was the exact question neither of Victoria's columns had asked. She wrote it at the bottom of the pad in capitals.

Brielle arrived at four with her own notes, having chosen the opposite strategy, all passion and no doctrine, planning to argue that truth should win because truth should win. "That's not how it works," Victoria said, and then softened, because Brielle's want was plain: she needed this panel to go well because her scholarship interview was Monday and she wanted a story to tell about it. "Here, look at this." She held up the card. "Say the exact word in your opening. Actual malice. Then define it fast, known false or reckless disregard, and the judges can't dock you." Brielle copied it, asked whether an error could ever be reckless if the deadline was midnight, and for ten minutes the two of them argued on the porch about deadlines and verification while the grandmother listened with her hands folded, pleased as a judge.

By dusk Victoria had something that was not a resolution but a position, held loosely. The newspaper probably should win under the rule, and the rule was probably right, because officials could too easily punish honest mistakes, and yet the mayor's side was not foolish, because recklessness could hide inside a busy newsroom like a stone inside bread. What she could not settle, and said so to Brielle, was where carelessness stopped and reckless disregard began, and whether a line like that could ever be drawn by anyone with an agenda.

On Monday she stood before Mr. Yang and the panel and argued the newspaper first, admitting the error in her first breath, then proving the reporter had made three calls before the story ran. Then she sat down, turned her legal pad over, and stood again as the mayor's counsel. "Actual malice," she said, "can be proven by what the reporter chose not to know." Then she clicked to her next card.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
Edouard had failed the biology quiz twice, and his mother had arranged a deal with Ms. Nur, the neighbour whose small farm sat behind the county road: mornings of work in exchange for afternoons of tutoring under the pecan trees. He arrived the first Saturday with his textbook wrapped in a feed-store bag because the zipper on his backpack had broken, and Ms. Nur pointed him to the cucumber rows without ceremony. The work was simple enough, weeding and hauling, and while his hands moved his mind kept circling the same stubborn paragraph, the one about how a cell reads its own instructions.

The trouble was that Edouard understood things best when he could hold them, and DNA was nothing he could hold. He had tried drawing it, reciting it, even recording himself on his phone and playing it back while he fell asleep, and the words slid off him the way water slid off the waxed hood of his mother's car. His friend Camilo, who had passed the quiz easily, told him to stop trying to picture it and just memorize the steps, while Quintin insisted the opposite, that nothing stuck unless you built it out of something physical, even pasta. Edouard had taken both suggestions and remained stuck between them, unsure whether his problem was memory or imagination.

On the second Saturday, Ms. Nur found him muttering the words codon and anticodon to himself as he stirred the compost. The smell that rose from the heap was noxious enough to make his eyes sting, but he kept working, and she watched him for a while before she spoke. "You're trying to carry it all in your head at once," she said. "Some things want to be externalized. Come to the garden after lunch."

After lunch she led him to the community plot on the far side of the barn, where a long table had been set between the tomato stakes. From a seed tin she poured out a handful of paper squares, each marked with three letters, and a second handful marked with amino acid names. "My granddaughter left these from her college class," Ms. Nur said. "She had your same trouble." She laid a strip of paper along the table's edge and wrote three letters on it, then handed Edouard a card. "You are a transfer RNA now. Each card carries one amino acid, and it has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA strip." She tapped the strip. "Find your match."

He turned the card over in his fingers. C C A, with the amino acid glycine written beneath in pencil. He walked the length of the strip, reading codons aloud, until he found G G U, and when he set his card against it the letters faced each other like two hands about to clasp. "It's backwards," he said slowly. "The card reads one way and the strip reads the other, but they fit." Ms. Nur only handed him another card. Camilo, who had ridden his bike over to see where Edouard disappeared to every weekend, picked up a card of his own and started hunting the strip, and then Quintin arrived, and soon the three of them were moving up and down the table, passing labelled cards to each other, one amino acid at a time, a slow chain of boys assembling something they could not see the end of.

That evening Edouard wrote to his cousin in the city, because a letter felt like the right container for what he wanted to say. "Dear Theo," he began. "I held a piece of a cell today, or the next thing to it. Every card carried exactly one amino acid and matched one codon on the strip, and I understood, standing there in the dirt, that reading DNA is not one magical act but thousands of small correct pairings. Camilo was right that the steps matter. Quintin was right that the hands matter. I think I needed both. What I still don't understand is how the cell knows where to start, and I have decided that is all right. I will learn that next Saturday."

On Monday he asked Ms. Nur, as they mended the fence by the goat pen, whether she thought understanding was something a person ever finished. She wound wire around a post before answering. "My granddaughter says consciousness is the brain noticing itself," she said. "Noticing what you don't understand is the same kind of thing, I'd say. It's how you know where to reach next." Edouard considered this while he hammered, and found it did not close the question so much as make the question comfortable to carry.

The third quiz came a week later. Edouard wrote the steps of transcription, then translation, then drew the strip and the card facing each other, three letters against three letters, one amino acid riding on the back. When the graded paper returned, the mark at the top was higher than anything he had earned that term, and he folded it into the feed-store bag with his textbook. On Saturday he rode out to the farm with two friends behind him on their bikes, and Ms. Nur was already at the table in the garden, dealing out the paper squares like cards for a game only she knew the rules to. "Glycine," she said, holding one up. "Whose is it?"

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
Victoria opened her laptop at the kitchen table and set a glass of water far enough away that a spill would absolve her of nothing, since she had planned for it. The assignment from Mr. Hamdan was due Sunday night: a Book class in Java with private fields, getter methods, and a test that proved they worked. She had written classes before, small ones, but this was the first time she had to think about what a class was hiding from the rest of the program.

She typed the fields first. Private, the worksheet said, so nothing outside could reach in and change them. A String title, an int pages, a boolean available. Then the constructor, then the getters, then a little main method that made a Book and printed what came back. It felt like building a machine out of sentences, and she caught herself wondering whether the machine would know it was a machine.

Zara had come over an hour ago and was lying on the couch with her own laptop, ostensibly doing the same assignment. "Mine keeps saying null," Zara said without looking up. "Like the word null, printed right there."

"Show me," Victoria said, but Zara just turned the screen. Victoria read the code upside down, which was its own skill, and saw it: Zara's constructor took a title and pages but never set the available field, and her test printed it. Except Zara's test didn't print null. It printed false.

"Why does yours say false and mine says null?" Zara asked, turning around properly now.

Victoria looked at her own screen. Her constructor took title and pages too, and she had forgotten the same thing. She ran her test before answering, and there it was: title printed null, pages printed 0, available printed false. Three fields, none of them ever set, three different answers.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So it's not random. Numbers come back 0, the boolean comes back false, and the String..." She tapped the screen. "The String comes back null."

"So they do get set? By who?"

"By nobody. That's the strange part." She tried saying it the way Mr. Hamdan had once described a different idea, that the language has opinions about what nothing looks like. She remembered, suddenly, a flashback to her grandfather's garage, the summer she was nine. He had labeled every drawer and every bin, and the empty bin still had its label, SCREWS, even when it held nothing. She had asked him why, and he said a drawer without a label was just a hole in the wall. She hadn't understood then. Now she almost did. A field with nothing in it still had a type, and the type decided what nothing looked like: a number's nothing was 0, a boolean's nothing was false, an object's nothing was null.

"Are you having a stroke?" Zara asked. "You went quiet and did your grandfather face."

"There's a drawer thing. It doesn't translate." Victoria wrote a comment in her code anyway, three words, for herself. Then she fixed her constructor, setting all three fields, and ran the test again. Title, pages, true. The machine worked. It was less satisfying than she expected, because the interesting part had been the failure, the moment the program told her the truth about what she hadn't done.

Zara copied the fix without asking why it worked, which Victoria noticed and decided not to comment on. Two years ago she would have explained it, patiently, in the way that made people feel small. Andrea used to call that her perspicacious problem, not that Victoria was wrong, but that she was right out loud. She was trying to hold both ideas now: that explaining helped, and that sometimes people wanted to find it themselves, the way she had just found it. She wasn't sure yet how to tell which moment was which.

"Mr. Hamdan's going to ask why we test the getters at all," Zara said. "If the constructor sets everything, isn't it obvious?"

"Maybe the test isn't for the code," Victoria said. "Maybe it's for us." She looked at the printed null still sitting in her terminal history, scrolled up out of reach but not gone. Then she opened a new file and typed a fourth field, private String publisher, and left it out of the constructor on purpose, just to see it happen one more time.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Victor had told Zaina, twice, that he was an excellent skater, and this was true in the sense that he had once been an excellent skater, at age nine, for one entire winter, before growing eleven inches and forgetting where his feet were. He was also, he had told her, completely relaxed about tonight, which was true in the sense that he had changed his shirt four times and had practised saying "hey" in the hallway mirror until his sister told him to stop.

The rink sat behind the rec centre like a freezer with ambitions, its ice glowing under fluorescent tubes that hummed a note only Victor seemed to hear, or claimed to hear, since it gave him something to talk about. Zaina arrived in a green coat and mittens with reindeer on them, out of season and unapologetic. She laced her skates faster than he did, which he attributed to the mittens, and then to the laces, and finally to nothing at all.

"You said you were good," she said, watching him grip the boards like a man rescuing himself from a flood.

"I said I had experience," Victor said. "Those are different claims."

They went around the rink in slow, wobbling orbits, and somewhere on the third lap Zaina took his hand, and Victor's whole nervous system conducted a brief but virulent argument with itself about which finger went where. He had imagined this moment, sort of, in the general way you imagine things you don't believe will happen. He imagined it differently, though. In the imagined version he was graceful.

Flashback, then: ninth grade, health class, Ms. Mansour writing a single sentence on the board while Larry whispered to Victor that this was the unit where you learned nothing you didn't already know.
