Ms. Mansour, who had a reputation as Larry's personal nemesis because she once made him rewrite an essay in which every paragraph began with "basically," tapped the board and said only, "Consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given," and then, before anyone could snicker, "Yes, Larry, even holding hands." Victor had spent the rest of the period drawing a shark. The sentence had stayed, the way certain sentences do, folded up small in a pocket of the mind.

Back at the rink, the shark-drawing period felt very far away and also very near. They skated. They held hands. Zaina laughed at his expostulations about the buzzing lights, which he delivered with real passion, having made up most of them on the spot, and which she knew he was making up, which was possibly why she laughed. They bought hot chocolate that tasted mostly of warm. It was, Victor thought, going extremely well, and he was honest enough with himself, even mid-optimism, to note that he was not a reliable judge of this.

After, in the parking lot, under one orange lamp, Zaina stopped walking. The cold made their breath visible, little ghosts leaving them.

"So," she said. "I think I'd rather just say goodnight here, if that's okay."

Victor had a whole plan. The plan involved the diner, and more hot chocolate, possibly a joke he'd been saving since Tuesday. The plan had been yes, and it was hard not to expostulate, hard not to point out that she had, earlier, taken his hand.

"You can take it back," Zaina said, reading him, or reading his face, which was doing something complicated. "Consent. You can say yes and then change your mind, even after. Whenever. Even holding hands."

"I know," Victor said, and then, because honesty was cheaper than being caught, "I mean, I knew it. I'm just also being a tiny bit sulky about the diner."

"That's allowed," she said. "Sulking. In moderation."

"It's not sulky, it's disappointed with flair." He put his hands in his pockets, which was where they should have been all along, and stepped back half a step, on purpose, so she could see it. "Goodnight, Zaina. I had a good time. The part before the parking lot."

"The reindeer mittens thank you." She was already walking toward her car, and she called the last part over her shoulder, breath curling behind her like something let go on purpose. "Text me when you're home. If you want."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
The parking lot behind the gym still had the chalk lines from last month's car wash fundraiser, and Cameron stood on one of them while the ceremony inside went on without him. He had walked out twenty minutes early, cap in hand, before the principal could read his name. It wasn't that he didn't want the diploma. He wanted it badly enough that taking it felt like a kind of theft, because Quintin should have been in that gym too, and Quintin was instead leaning against a dented Civic three rows over, waiting for Cameron to notice him.

"You walked out on your own graduation," Quintin said. "That's the most you thing you've ever done."

"Somebody had to. You weren't using your seat."

Quintin laughed, but the laugh ran out fast, the way it had all spring. He'd left school in November, four credits short, for reasons he described differently every time Cameron asked: money, his mother's hours getting cut, a general disgust with desks. Since then he'd been applying for jobs, and Cameron had been listening, and the listening had become its own weight between them.

"I had an interview Tuesday," Quintin said. He picked at the antenna of the Civic, bending it and letting it spring back. "Warehouse place off Route 9. Guy looked at my application for about four seconds and asked if I had my diploma. I said I was finishing it. He said to come back when I was." He bent the antenna again. "I looked it up after. Did you know the unemployment rate last year, 2023, was 3.9 percent for people twenty-five and up with a high school diploma? And 5.6 percent for people without one." He said the numbers flat, like receipts. "Two points isn't the whole world. But it's the whole world at a warehouse."

Cameron had his own envelope in his jacket, the one they handed you at the door if you didn't want to cross the stage. He hadn't opened it. The paper inside was worth exactly what Quintin couldn't get, and he was honest enough with himself to know that his walking out hadn't been solidarity, it had been guilt dressed in a rented gown. His father's adage came back to him, the one about how doors don't lock themselves, and he'd always thought it was perspicacious until tonight, when he understood it was just a way of blaming the person standing outside.

"I go Monday to register for summer classes," Quintin said. "Adult ed. Two credits, done by December." He said it like a confession. "I told my mom I'd decide by tonight, though, because my uncle needs a hand at his shop upstate, starting next week, and he'll only hold the spot until tomorrow morning. Cash work. No diploma question, no interview, nothing."

"That's a job now," Cameron said.

"That's a job now," Quintin agreed. "And December is December." He looked toward the gym, where the muffled sound of applause rolled out every forty seconds like weather. "Here's what I can't get straight. If I go upstate, I'm working, I'm earning, and I'm still the guy without the diploma in every system that counts. If I stay and do the credits, I'm broke until winter and maybe still the guy, because the paper doesn't suture anything by itself. It doesn't fix the last year. It just changes which door I'm knocking on."

Cameron turned the envelope over in his hands. He thought about telling Quintin that the numbers cut both ways, that 3.9 meant most people without diplomas were still working, that the statistic measured groups and not one specific person standing in a parking lot with a bent antenna. He thought about telling him the opposite, that the gap was real and doors were doors. Both things were true at once and he couldn't crush them into one clean sentence, and he was tired of people who could.

"I don't know which one you should pick," Cameron said.

"Everyone's got an opinion except you."

"Everyone's got an opinion. I've got a fact and no opinion. The fact is the two numbers. The opinion part, I keep flip-flopping." He held out the envelope. "This isn't the answer. I know it's not transferable. But I want you to have something from tonight, and this is the only thing I've got on me."

Quintin looked at it and didn't take it. "Open it first."

Cameron tore the flap with his thumb. The diploma inside was heavier paper than he expected, the kind they made you believe in, his name printed in a font that looked almost like handwriting. He held it where the lot light could reach it, and Quintin leaned in and read it out loud, quietly, the way you read someone else's mail when they let you.

"Congratulations," Quintin said. "Really. That's yours. Nobody took it from me." He straightened the antenna one last time, then checked his phone. "I've got until morning to call my uncle." He got into the Civic and rolled the window down, arm hanging out, keys not yet in the ignition. "Walk with me to the gas station. I have to think out loud, and you're the only one who won't tell me what to think."

Cameron put the diploma back in his jacket, unzipped the gown, and dropped it over the chalk line as they walked.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
The flyer outside the library said Peer Feedback Workshop, Room 114, and Jessica had signed up because Ms. Thompson had looked at her across the lab table and said, "You have opinions. Say them where they count." She wasn't sure that counted as an invitation, but she'd taken it as one, and now she was sitting in a circle of chairs with a worksheet that asked her to rewrite the sentence "You ruined it" as something a person could actually hear.

Her group project was the problem, though she hadn't written that down. Amelia had promised the slides for their chemistry presentation by Tuesday, and they'd arrived Thursday night, an hour before Jessica and Viviane did their rehearsal in Jessica's kitchen. The presentation had gone to pieces anyway. Monday they'd present again, this time for a real grade, and Jessica had spent the weekend drafting versions of a conversation she hadn't had yet.

"You're on your sixth try," Viviane said, looking over her shoulder in the emptying library. "It's one sentence."

"It's not one sentence. Watch." Jessica read from the worksheet. "'Psychologist Thomas Gordon came up with I-messages back in the sixties as a way to raise a problem without blaming.' So instead of you ruined it, you say something like, I felt stuck when the slides came in late." She put the sheet down. "It sounds like a greeting card."

"You sound like a greeting card," Viviane said. "Amelia doesn't."

They tried it in the library carrel, Viviane playing Amelia, slouching with her chin in her hand the way Amelia slouched. "Amelia, I felt stuck when the slides came in late, because we couldn't rehearse." Viviane dropped the slouch immediately. "Okay, that's not terrible. But you said because we couldn't rehearse. Say what it cost you, not the group. Otherwise it's still a committee talking."

Jessica crossed out a line. The chemistry unit they were presenting was on allotropes, the different forms a single element could take, carbon as graphite and carbon as diamond, and she'd been struck by how the same material became unrecognizable under pressure. She didn't say this out loud. She wrote, I felt stuck when the slides came in late, and I stayed up past one redoing the timing.

"That's specific," Viviane said. "But you still haven't said what you want."

"Wanting something from Amelia feels like an ambush."

"Then ambush her kindly."

Sunday night Jessica found Ms. Thompson stacking chairs in Room 114, the workshop having run long. Ms. Thompson was known to be irascible about people who left chairs unstacked, so Jessica stacked two before speaking. "The worksheet thing. The I-messages. Does it work when the person already thinks you're mad at them?"

"Depends whether you're mad at her." Ms. Thompson set down the last chair. "Gordon's idea is older than I am. It survives because it's honest about whose feelings these are. It falls apart when people use it as a costume." She picked up her bag. "Say the true part first. Kindness can't be a structure you hide behind."

Jessica walked home turning that over. She'd wanted a formula, a way to be honest without paying for it, and Ms. Thompson had refused to hand her one. Maybe the method wasn't a shield; maybe it was just a door, and you still had to walk through it carrying whatever you actually felt.

Monday morning, twenty minutes before first period, Amelia was at the lab table taping a flash drive to a printout. Jessica stood across from her and said, "I felt stuck when the slides came in late. I stayed up past one redoing the timing, and I was scared of the grade. I'm not asking you to apologize. I'm asking what happened."

Amelia's hands stopped on the tape. "My dad moved out last month. I kept meaning to." She turned the flash drive over once. "I did finish them, though. Both versions. Pick whichever."

Jessica sat down and took the drive. On the screen, the slide on allotropes had been rebuilt with a diagram she'd never seen, cleaner than anything she'd drafted. She looked at it for a long moment, then at Amelia, then back at the diagram. "This one," she said. "But you're explaining this slide, not me."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Cohen turned the chicken over in its plastic tray and listened to the hiss of the ovens behind him. The community kitchen on Delancey ran three nights a week out of a church basement, and tonight he had the long steel counter nearest the sink, the one his mother preferred because you could see the door from it. His father was on days now and his mother on nights, which meant that for the first time the Sunday meal was his, and he had promised them roast chicken, potatoes, and the green beans with garlic that his grandmother used to make. He had promised it over text.

That morning his sister had sent him a message from her dorm, since she had a habit of checking on him without admitting she was checking. "Don't wash the chicken," she wrote. "I know Dad always does. I used to too. The CDC actually advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces. Cook it to temp and you're fine. Take a pic of the thermometer for me." He had read it twice, standing in the hallway with his shoes still on, because his father had rinsed chicken under the tap for as long as Cohen could remember, holding each piece under the stream with tongs while the water drummed against the steel, and it had always seemed like the careful thing, the clean thing, the first step of a serious cook.

At the counter beside him, Sukhman was cubing potatoes with a virtuoso's economy, the knife barely lifting, and Josie was snapping the ends off green beans into a colander with more force than the beans required. She had been quiet since they arrived, and Cohen knew why, because he had been the one who told Mr. Almeida that Josie had taken the last of the paprika from the shared spice shelf and not replaced it. He had thought he was being helpful. He had since done the arithmetic on that.

"So are you going to rinse it or not," Sukhman said, without looking up from the potatoes. He had watched Cohen take the chicken out, watched him look at the sink, watched him not move.

"My sister says the CDC advises against it. Splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces." Cohen set the tray down. "But my dad did it my whole life and nobody got sick."

"My mom still does it," Sukhman said. "She says the American way of cooking leaves the blood in." He shrugged with one shoulder, still cubing. "It's not blood, it's myoglobin, but I don't tell her that."

Josie snapped a bean in half. "You could just pat it dry," she said, not to Cohen exactly, but to the colander. "Paper towels. That's what the actual cooks here do."

Mr. Almeida came around the end of the aisle with a clipboard, checking oven assignments. He was the volunteer who ran Sunday nights, a retired line cook with forearms like rope, and he paused at their counter long enough to see the chicken sitting raw in its tray, dry, unwashed. "Good," he said. "Season it, truss it if you know how, and it goes in at four twenty-five." Then he moved on, and Cohen felt something in his chest unclench, though he could not have said whether it was approval or just the relief of not having to decide alone.

He patted the bird dry with paper towels, the way Josie had said, and salted it inside and out, and his hands learned the odd intimacy of the work, slipping herbs under the skin where the fat had gone soft and friable at the edges of the cold flesh. He kept thinking about his father at the sink, tongs and drumming water, and how his father would probably keep doing it, and how a person could hold a practice for thirty years and love the person who taught it to him and still be wrong about the practice, and how being wrong about it had cost nothing so far, which was not the same as costing nothing. He did not think you could prove anything to a man with a memory of his mother's kitchen. He did not think it was his job to try.

The chicken went into the oven, and the potatoes, and Josie moved down the counter to him without a word and began trimming the garlic, thin slivers, faster than he would have done it. "I replaced the paprika," she said, crushing a clove under the flat of the knife. "It came yesterday."

"I shouldn't have said anything," Cohen said.

"You shouldn't have said it to him before you said it to me." She scraped the garlic into the pan, and the oil took it, and the smell rose up over the whole basement, over the steam of the dishwashing station and the vinegar of the salad table. She looked at him for a second. "But it was true."

When his mother came at seven, she stood at the door a moment before he saw her, coat still on, watching him pull the roasting pan from the oven with the folded towels Mr. Almeida had taught them to use. He set it on the steel, and the skin had gone the color of dark honey, and the thermometer in the thigh read the number his sister had demanded, so he took the picture. His mother sat down across from him and pulled her plate close.

"You didn't wash it," she said.

"No," Cohen said, and carved the first slice, and offered it to her on the flat of the knife.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.
story:
The elevator in the new building smelled like onions and floor polish, and it took forty seconds to travel five floors, which Audrey knew because she counted. She counted the boxes in the hallway too: eleven, her mother's handwriting on four of them, her own on seven. Their old apartment had been on the ground floor of a walk-up, where Sally used to knock on the kitchen window instead of using the door.

That was the arrangement they'd made in sixth grade, before either of them could have explained why it mattered. Sally would tap twice on the glass, and Audrey would slide the window up, and they would pass a bag of chips or a library book or, one memorably terrible week in eighth grade, a series of folded notes about Elliana's birthday party and who had and had not been invited. On the last morning before the movers came, Sally had tapped twice on the glass out of habit, then laughed, then stopped laughing. "I'll text you every day," she said. That had been nine days ago. She had texted five times.

The new school assigned Audrey a locker on the third floor next to a girl named Elliana, which felt like a joke the universe was telling only to her. This Elliana was not the Elliana; she was taller, with a chipped front tooth, and she had lived here her whole life. On the second day she watched Audrey wrestle a stuck lock and said, "Hit it with the flat of your hand, not your fist. Everyone learns that by October." Audrey hit it with the flat of her hand and the lock opened.

The apartment was on the fifth floor, third door from the elevator. Their neighbor across the hall was Ms. Teo, who taught piano and left her door propped open while she practiced, so that Audrey came to know Chopin before she knew anything else about the building. Ms. Teo had knocked the first evening with a plate of pineapple tarts and a warning that the hot water ran cold if anyone in 5B showered first. "Learn the schedule," she said, "and the building will subsume you eventually. It does that to everyone." Audrey had looked the word up later, unsure whether it was a threat or a comfort.

The hardest part was not the school, which was fine, or the apartment, which was bigger than the old one. The hardest part was Tuesday nights, because Tuesday had been the night she and Sally walked to the twenty-four-hour laundromat with Sally's mother, who was saving for a washer and couldn't quite manage it on her penurious grocery-store wages, and the three of them folded towels while the dryers tumbled and the fluorescents buzzed. There was no laundromat here. There was a washer in the hallway closet that hummed like a refrigerator. Audrey had stood in front of it last Tuesday with a load of towels in her arms and not put them in.

She tried to explain this to her mother once, who said, "You can fold towels anywhere, sweetheart," which was technically true and completely beside the point. What Audrey could not say was that she felt foolish. She was sixteen. She had wanted the move, even, had said so out loud at dinner last spring when her mother got the job offer, had argued for it with actual reasons. And now she was lying awake missing a laundromat. Missing a bus route. Missing the particular way their old building's radiator clanked at eleven. She had not told Sally any of this, because Sally's five texts were full of parties and gossip and the new girl who had taken Audrey's seat in French, and because Sally seemed, from her messages, entirely unscathed.

It was Elliana, at the lockers on a Thursday, who broke the silence. Audrey had said something offhand, "I can't wait for October," meaning it as a joke about the weather, and then heard herself and added, quieter, "Actually, that's a lie. I miss my old building so much it's embarrassing." Elliana snapped her own lock shut and shrugged one shoulder. "My cousin researches this stuff at her university. Homesickness. She says basically everybody who goes somewhere new misses something about home, and around twenty percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale." She pulled a textbook out of her bag. "So it's not just you being weird. Twenty percent is like one in five, and those are just the ones who admit it on a form."

Audrey stood with her hand still on her open locker. "Twenty percent," she said.

"At or above the midpoint," Elliana said. "The midpoint of a severity scale. I'm not doing the math wrong; I asked her twice." She smiled with her chipped tooth. "I cried for the first month at band camp, if that helps. Nobody had told me the statistic yet."

That evening Audrey sat on the floor of her room with her phone, and before she could think better of it she typed the true thing: I miss the laundromat. I miss Tuesday. I miss you and it's embarrassing how much. She stared at it for a long time, the cursor blinking, and then she thought about the fact that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, whole buildings full of people quietly missing radiators and bus routes and particular windows, all of them assuming they were the only one. She pressed send and put the phone face-down on the carpet.

The reply came while she was running the towels, the first load, finally, in the humming closet machine. Three taps, Sally had written, just the words. Audrey read it standing in the hallway with wet hands, then walked to the kitchen, slid the window up, and leaned out into the October air, five floors above a street she was only beginning to know.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a).
story:
Claire had drawn the same parabola eleven times, and eleven times it came out looking like a doorway. The assignment from Ms. Leblanc was due at midnight: estimate the area under the curve of x squared between zero and three, using at least twenty rectangles. She had built a spreadsheet, dragged the formula down two hundred rows, and now the rectangles marched across the page like fence palings, each one too narrow to read without squinting. The sum of their areas sat in a single cell at the bottom: 9.045. Ms. Leblanc's instruction, in her flat and famously unsentimental voice, had been that the answer was supposed to be an estimate. Nobody had said what to do if you wanted the real one.

She texted Sydney, who replied with a photograph of her own spreadsheet, captioned "120 rectangles and I still have to do the reading for epidemiology, this class is a scam." Sydney's estimate was 9.0375. Closer, obviously, because more rectangles meant less leftover sliver at each edge, but Claire found she couldn't stop staring at the gap between them, the small wrongness of it. Her father came through the kitchen with a laundry basket and asked, without slowing down, whether she'd eaten the last of the good bread. She said she hadn't, which was true, and he said okay, and the door to the basement stairs thumped shut behind him. She turned back to the fence palings.

Ayman called at nine, out of breath from his run. "Are you doing the rectangle thing?"

"Two hundred rectangles," Claire said. "It's nine point something."

"Sydney's doing four hundred. She says she's going to do a thousand if it kills her." He was unwrapping something, foil crackling against the phone's microphone. "My cousin had Ms. Leblanc two years ago. He said she marks hard on the write-up, not the number. She likes it when you say what you did wrong."

Claire pulled the phone away from her ear and looked at it, then at the spreadsheet. Somewhere in the middle of the two hundred rows there was a column she'd labeled "height" and a column labeled "width," and below those a third column nobody had asked for, where she'd been playing with the running total out of pure boredom. She'd typed a formula that added each rectangle's area to the one before it, so the total climbed as you went down the page: the area from zero up to one, then up to two, then up to three. She had accidentally built a function. Each row was the area so far, and each row was a little bigger than the row above it, and the little bit it grew by, row to row, was exactly the height of the rectangle in that row.

She put the phone on the counter, speaker on, and started writing on the back of her physics handout. If she made a function F out of those running totals, then the height of the curve at each point, the f she'd been reading off the parabola all night, was the amount by which F grew. She wrote F is an antiderivative of f, copying the word from a glossary at the back of her textbook, and underneath it she wrote the whole thing out plainly: the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. Two evaluations. One subtraction. For x squared from zero to three, she didn't even need the spreadsheet, just the antiderivative, which the textbook's table gave her, and then the value at three, minus the value at zero.

"Are you still there?" Ayman said.

"Hold on." She did the arithmetic twice. Nine. Exactly nine, no decimal, no fence palings, and her two hundred rectangles had said 9.045, which meant the rectangles weren't the answer at all, they were scaffolding you were supposed to kick away. Sydney's thousand rectangles would get closer and closer to nine and never be permitted to arrive, and the thing that let you arrive was sitting in one line of the textbook Claire had skipped past because it looked like notation and not like news. The whole night of dragging formulas had been a way of approaching a door that had been open the entire time. It underpinned everything Ms. Leblanc had done that semester, Claire realized, all the velocity graphs and distance graphs, the way the class kept drawing the same pair of shapes over and over with arrows between them.

"It's nine," she said into the phone. "Exactly. There's a shortcut, it's in chapter five, I think she assigned it to be cruel."

Ayman laughed. "She assigned it so Sydney would build a thousand rectangles."

"She's going to. She'll be so mad." Claire opened her chat with Sydney, typed the shortcut out in full, antiderivative and all, and held her thumb over the send button. It felt, briefly, like taking something from Sydney, the four hundred rectangles, the epidemiology reading being sacrificed to them, the whole bombatic misery of it that Sydney was enjoying more than she would ever admit. Claire deleted the last sentence of the message and retyped it. She hit send, then turned back to her write-up and wrote, at the top of a fresh page, "The estimate was 9.045. The exact answer is 9. Here is why they differ," and left the pen resting in the gutter of the page while the message delivered, delivered, and was read.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form.
story:
The job offer sat in Audrey's inbox like a bill she hadn't opened yet. Subject line: "Welcome to the team! Please complete onboarding." Below that, a link, and below the link, in gray font the color of an apology, the words "By proceeding you agree to all terms and conditions." Audrey read it three times, then looked at her ceiling as if the terms might be written up there in friendlier language.

The job was at Halvorsen's, the garden center two bus transfers away, eleven dollars an hour plus a discount that would catalyze her incipient plans for a window garden and, more urgently, her plan to stop asking her mother for money. She had interviewed on Tuesday with a man in a fleece vest who called everything "a value-add," including the break room. Now the onboarding portal wanted her to check a box confirming she had read a liability waiver, a noncompete clause, and something called an arbitration agreement, which she gathered meant that if Halvorsen's ever wronged her, she would be wronged in a venue of their choosing.

The problem, as Audrey framed it to Ziad over chat, was not that she objected to any particular term. It was that she couldn't tell what she was actually doing. "I click a box," she typed. "Is that signing? My dad signs things with a pen and makes a little ceremony of it. This is me, in my pajamas, clicking."

Ziad, who was doing his own college forms and had developed opinions, replied within seconds. "It counts. There's a whole law. The ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form."

"That sounds like something you found on a forum."

"I found it on a government site, actually, but keep being suspicious."

Audrey opened a new tab and typed the words in herself, because trusting Ziad's summaries had burned her before, once catastrophically, in a group project on the Brontës. The law was there, exactly as he'd said. She sat back. So the click counted. The ceremony, the pen, her father's little flourish, all of it was theater; the law did not care about ink. Somehow this was less comforting than she'd expected. A signature was supposed to be a moment of consent, a pause where a person weighed things. Hers had been shrunk to the same gesture she used to dismiss a cookie notice.

She scrolled the terms again, slower now, feeling the weight of what she'd learned. The liability waiver said she released Halvorsen's from claims arising from ordinary risks, including but not limited to forklifts. The noncompete said she wouldn't work at a competing garden center within ten miles for a year, which was funny, since she could name exactly one other garden center and it was a hardware store with three sad rose bushes out front. Her economics teacher had a saying, an epigram she'd repeated until the class could recite it in unison: "Read what you sign, because it will read you back." Audrey had always thought it was corny. On screen, at 10:47 on a school night, it was less corny.

She called Leighton, who had worked at a bakery and therefore had opinions about waivers. "I signed one about the ovens," Leighton said. "Then I burned my wrist on a pan and nobody made me arbitration anything, they just gave me a burn kit with cartoon bears on it. So the terrifying document is mostly for the terrifying situations that never happen."

"That's not a legal argument. That's a bear-shaped anecdote."

"It's my whole philosophy, actually."

Audrey hung up and looked at the box again, unpainted, unadorned, waiting. She thought about Ms. Popescu downstairs, who had lived in the building for thirty years and still kept her lease in a drawer, paper with actual signatures, hers and a landlord who had died in 2009. When the building changed hands last spring, Ms. Popescu had carried that paper to the office like a relic and come home satisfied. Paper had worked for her. But Audrey understood now that the paper itself had never been the point. The point was that the law recognized a person's agreement however it arrived, and therefore a person had to actually agree, deliberately, before the gesture. The box was honest in a way the ceremony wasn't. It offered nothing, no pen, no flourish, no pause. The pause had to be supplied by her.

So she supplied it. She scrolled to the bottom, found the decline option in small type, and clicked that instead. No terms, no forklifts, no cartoon bear burn kits. Then she opened a message to Ziad: "Turns out declining counts too. Same law, working in the other direction."

Before she could close the laptop, a new email arrived from Halvorsen's, subject line "Confirmation of your onboarding decision," and beneath the greeting, in the same gray font, the sentence: "This email constitutes notice and shall be considered received upon delivery." Below it, a single line of body text and a link labeled "Click here to acknowledge receipt."

Audrey stared at it for a long moment, then laughed, alone, in her pajamas.

"Unbelievable," she said to the screen. "It's boxes all the way down."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change.
story:
The sealed tubes arrived from the supply catalogue looking like nothing much, four inches of glass with a stubborn brownish color inside, but Sadie had spent two weeks learning what they were about to do. Her project for the regional science fair was a prediction, written and sealed in an envelope the night before, about how the gas inside would answer a hot water bath. She had typed the prediction at her kitchen table while her mother dried dishes, and she had not let herself soften the language. Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change. Heating the tube was the disturbance. Therefore the system would shift in whatever direction consumed the heat, and the color would tell her which direction that was.

The trouble began at seven forty in the morning, in the gymnasium with its folded-away bleachers and its smell of floor wax. Tube one, lowered into the beaker of hot water, refused to change. Sadie counted to sixty under her breath. Matis, who had come early to set up his own project on pond turbidity, leaned over the partition between their tables and said, "It's not doing anything."

"I know."

"Is that bad?"

She lifted the tube out, dried it, held it beside the control tube she'd left on the table. Identical. Which meant either she had predicted wrong, which she could survive, or something was wrong with the tube, which felt worse because it wasn't hers to be wrong about. She uncapped the hot water bath and checked the thermometer anyway, in case she was the one who was wrong in the simplest possible way. Sixty-eight degrees. That was fine.

There was a note in the side pocket of her display board, folded into a small square, which she'd found taped to her locker on Friday. She read it again now, partly for luck. "Sadie," Matis's handwriting ran, "I looked up what you told me about the equilibrium thing and I think I finally get it, the part where it only partly counteracts the change. The system pushes back but it doesn't win. Anyway if your tube does nothing tomorrow, check the seal before you check your brain. Reilly says the ones from the old chem room are half junk. Don't tell Reilly I said she said that. Good luck. M." She had read it four times since Friday, once in the bus, and it had sensitized her, more than she'd admitted, to the possibility that her equipment rather than her reasoning was the weak point.

Reilly arrived at eight twenty with a coffee she wasn't supposed to have and looked at the two identical tubes for approximately three seconds. "Those are from the storage room," she said. "The senior chem lab got new ones last year. Those are, what's the word, obsolescent."

"Obsolete," Sadie said.

"Obsolescent. On their way out. Still technically alive, like the vice principal." Reilly picked up tube one and turned it under the light, and at a certain angle there was a faint sheen at the joint between glass and seal, a whisper of a gap. "That's your problem. It's not sealed. Gas has been sneaking out since before you were born, probably."

Sadie sat back on her heels. She felt two things at once and could not make them the same feeling. One was deflation: the whole demonstration was a dud, and judges were going to walk past her table at nine. The other was a strange, almost unwanted relief, because if the tube was open to the room then it wasn't a closed system at equilibrium at all, and a system that wasn't at equilibrium couldn't be expected to shift like one. Her prediction might still be right. It just hadn't been tested. She understood, in a way she hadn't at her kitchen table, the difference between being wrong and being untested, and she understood also that she couldn't simply declare the second one, because she had no proof yet, only Reilly's sheen at a certain angle.

"Can we get to the senior lab before nine?" she asked.

"Ms. Grewal has the key," Reilly said. "She's doing check-in at the door."

Ms. Grewal was at the folding table by the gym entrance with a clipboard and a lanyard and the unhurried manner of someone who had supervised eleven of these fairs. When Sadie explained, quickly, about the seal and the sheen and the sealed envelope with the prediction in it, Ms. Grewal didn't lecture and didn't soften it. "You want fresh tubes and you want them documented as fresh," she said, writing a hall pass. "The ones in the cabinet, second shelf, delivered in the fall. Take two. Label them. If you're going to claim your prediction held, you claim it on tubes that couldn't fail you any other way." She handed over the pass. "Nine minutes."

They ran. The hallway smelled like the morning announcements speakers, faintly warm and dusty. In the senior lab Matis held the flashlight while Sadie checked the joints of both new tubes against the light, one after the other, then again, then wrote the batch numbers on her wrist in ballpoint because she'd left her notebook at the fair table. Back in the gym, with eight minutes to spare, she lowered the new tube into the bath, and this time the color deepened within seconds, clearly, unmistakably, the tube going darker beside its pale control like a slow argument resolving.

She taped the prediction envelope, unopened, to the corner of her board, next to the batch numbers and the photographs of the failed tube's worn seal, because the failed tube was part of the story too. What stayed uncertain, and she knew it, was whether the shift she'd predicted was exactly the shift she'd gotten; the color told her direction, and direction was what the principle promised, but she had no numbers, and a judge with numbers could take her apart. She would say that if asked. Matis appeared at her shoulder as the first judges started down the aisle, and she pinched the envelope's edge between two fingers and looked at him.

"Want to do the honors?"

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Since 1975, ending most debate in the US Senate through cloture has required three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.
story:
The folding chairs were already warm when Layla sat down between Eli and his little brother's empty booster seat, which he'd claimed as a place for his backpack. The town hall meeting had been called about the Millbrook Pathway Bill, the one that would fund a walking trail between the high school and the library, and the room smelled of burnt coffee and the rain everyone had tracked in on their shoes. Layla had come because her mother had come, and because she wanted, privately, to see whether the thing her civics teacher called "the process" looked anything like a process up close, or whether it was just people talking until they were tired.

Mr. Xu, who taught chemistry and served on the town council, stood at the front with a clipboard and a microphone that whined whenever he shifted his weight. He explained that the bill had been drafted by a committee of residents and council members, that it had gone through two readings, and that tonight was the public hearing before the final vote. "So it's almost a law," Eli whispered, and Layla shushed him, though she had been thinking the same thing, that the word "almost" did a lot of work in a sentence like that.

A man in a rain jacket stood up first and said the trail would take parking spaces from his shop, and that the town had no right to give away what it had charged him taxes on. Then a woman stood and said her daughter had nearly been hit crossing Route 9 twice this year, and that asphalt was cheaper than a funeral. Neither of them looked at the other. Layla wrote both arguments in her notebook, side by side, and then drew a line between them, because she had learned in debate club that two things could both be true and still not fit in the same sentence.

Louis-Philippe arrived late, shaking water off his coat, and slid into the seat on her other side. He leaned over and said, "Did you hear about the federal one? The trail maintenance bill, in the Senate. It had fifty-five votes and it still died." Layla said that didn't make sense; fifty-five was more than half of a hundred. "That's what I said," Louis-Philippe told her. "Ask him."

She didn't want to ask him. She wanted to work it out herself, so while the council debated an amendment about lighting along the trail, she did the arithmetic in the margin of her notebook, dividing a hundred by five and getting twenty, then multiplying by three and getting sixty. Sixty was more than fifty-five. Something in the Senate's rules, then, put the bar higher than a majority for ending debate, which meant a bill could have more supporters than opponents and still never reach a vote. She underlined the number twice, and beside it she wrote "cloture," a word she half remembered from a textbook chapter she'd skimmed, and next to that she wrote a question mark, because memory was not the same as knowledge.

When Mr. Xu opened the floor for general questions, she stood up before she could talk herself out of it. "Mr. Xu, the federal trail bill had fifty-five senators supporting it. Why did it fail?" The microphone picked up her voice and made it sound flatter than it felt in her chest.

Mr. Xu's expression turned saturnine, heavy and serious in a way she hadn't expected from a man who made potassium jokes in third period. "Since 1975, ending most debate in the Senate takes three-fifths of the senators. With all hundred seats filled, that's sixty votes for cloture. Fifty-five wasn't enough." He said it in one breath, without editorializing, and sat back down, and Layla wrote it out in full this time, all of it, because she had the sense that she'd just been handed something she would need later.

Eli passed her a folded note. "so 55 votes = losing?" She wrote back, "55 votes = not enough to end the debate. different thing," and passed it across the booster seat, and Eli read it, frowned, and nodded slowly, the way he did in physics when a formula finally loosened.

The council clerk then read a letter into the record, from their state senator, who could not attend. "Dear neighbors," the clerk read, her voice careful with every comma, "I supported the Millbrook Pathway Bill at the state level, and I watched a version of it die in committee last spring, not because a majority opposed it, but because our procedures adumbrate their outcomes before any vote is taken. The shape of a rule can foreshadow the shape of a result. I encourage you to look closely at your own procedures tonight. Democracy is mostly plumbing." A few people laughed at the last line. Layla didn't. She was thinking about her line drawn between the shopkeeper and the mother, and about whether the trail itself was the point, or whether the point was that they were all standing in a room arguing about it.

She raised her hand again, and when Mr. Xu nodded at her, she said, "Before we vote, could the council say which version of the bill is actually being voted on? Because if the amendment about the lights changes what people thought they were supporting, then we're not really voting on the same thing the committee drafted." The room went quiet in a way that felt like held breath. The man in the rain jacket turned around in his chair and looked at her, and so did the mother.

Mr. Xu looked down at his clipboard for a long moment. "That's a fair question," he said. "Clerk, read the bill as amended, in full."

The clerk began to read, and Layla sat back down, took out her pen, and drew a small square around the number sixty in the margin of her notebook, then another square around the word cloture, and waited, listening, while the words of the bill moved one more time through the room.
